title: Primary Care Approach to Men's Health
source: Seminar 5 Primary Care Approach to Men’s Health.pdf

topics.NCD: NCDs in men, IHD, smoking & alcohol

cards.q: What is a non-communicable disease (NCD)?
cards.a:
• A **chronic disease** of **long duration**
• Results from a **combination** of **genetic, physiological, environmental and behavioural** factors
• Not transmitted person to person
cards.m: NCD = 'Not Caught, Developed' over years

cards.q: What are the four main types of NCD (WHO)?
cards.a:
• **Cardiovascular diseases** (IHD, stroke)
• **Cancers**
• **Chronic respiratory diseases** (COPD, asthma)
• **Diabetes**
cards.m: Heart, Tumour, Lungs, Sugar

cards.q: List the four key modifiable risk factors for NCDs named on the slides.
cards.a:
• **Unhealthy diet**
• **Smoking** (tobacco use)
• **Alcohol** consumption
• **Sedentary lifestyle** (physical inactivity)
cards.m: The 'big four' behaviours that a KK lifestyle clinic targets

cards.q: WHO 2021: how many people died of an NCD before age 70, and which NCD group causes the most NCD deaths?
cards.a:
• **18 million** NCD deaths occurred **before age 70** (premature)
• **Cardiovascular disease** causes the most NCD deaths (**at least 19 million** deaths in 2021)
• Note: slide wording merges the two figures; 19 million is the CVD total, 18 million the under-70 total
cards.m: Under-70 = 18 M; CVD = 19 M

cards.q: NHMS 2023: are diabetes, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia more prevalent in Malaysian men or women?
cards.a:
• Slightly **lower in men**: DM **15.0 vs 16.2%**, HPT **28.8 vs 29.6%**, cholesterol **30.5 vs 36.3%**
• Depression also lower in men (**3.9 vs 5.4%**) - likely **under-diagnosed**
• Yet men have **higher CVD mortality** - they are screened and treated less, and present later
cards.m: Similar prevalence, worse outcome = men are missed, not spared

cards.q: On the NCD table, colorectal carcinoma shows 17.5% in men vs 11.3% in women. What does this figure actually mean?
cards.a:
• It is the **proportion of all cancers** that are colorectal (Malaysia National Cancer Registry 2017-2021), not a population prevalence
• CRC is the **most common cancer in Malaysian men**
• Note: slide labels it 'prevalence (%)'; correct reading is share of cancer cases
cards.m: About 1 in 6 cancers in Malaysian men is colorectal

cards.q: What is the leading cause of death in Malaysian males (DOSM)?
cards.a:
• **Ischaemic heart disease** - about **15.3%** of medically certified male deaths
• Shares risk factors with ED, LUTS and many cancers: smoking, DM, HPT, obesity
cards.m: Men die of their hearts first

cards.q: Give three reasons why ischaemic heart disease is more common in men.
cards.a:
• **More smoking and alcohol** on top of DM and hypertension
• **Fewer regular check-ups** (**53.8%** of men vs **60.8%** of women)
• **Lower oestrogen** - men lack its cardioprotective effect
cards.m: Smoke, Skip check-ups, Short of oestrogen

cards.q: Why does oestrogen protect against ischaemic heart disease (why men lose this protection)?
cards.a:
• Raises **HDL** and lowers **LDL** cholesterol
• Promotes **nitric oxide-mediated vasodilatation** and healthy endothelium
• Men lack this throughout adult life; women lose it after **menopause**, when their risk catches up
cards.m: Oestrogen = natural statin plus vasodilator

cards.q: GATS Malaysia 2023: what proportion of Malaysian men are current smokers?
cards.a:
• About **35.7%** of men are current smokers - far higher than women
• Smoking drives IHD, COPD, lung, bladder and colorectal cancer, and **ED**
cards.m: Roughly 1 in 3 Malaysian men smokes

cards.q: Which occupational exposures raise men's risk of chronic lung disease?
cards.a:
• **Asbestos** (asbestosis, mesothelioma, lung cancer)
• **Silica dust** (silicosis - quarrying, construction, sandblasting)
• Also diesel exhaust and coal dust
• Always take an **occupational history** in a breathless man
cards.m: Men do the dusty jobs

cards.q: NHMS 2023: what share of Malaysians who drank excessively in the past 12 months were men, and which chronic disease does alcohol drive?
cards.a:
• **75%** of excessive drinkers were **men**
• Alcohol is the **key driver of chronic liver disease** (fatty liver to alcoholic hepatitis to cirrhosis)
• Also linked to HPT, cardiomyopathy, cancers and injury
cards.m: 3 of every 4 heavy drinkers are men

cards.q: Smoker at a Klinik Kesihatan: what is the structured brief intervention and first-line pharmacotherapy?
cards.a:
• **5 A's**: **Ask, Advise, Assess** readiness, **Assist**, **Arrange** follow-up
• Pharmacotherapy: **NRT** (patch + short-acting gum/lozenge) or **varenicline**
• Refer to **KK Quit Smoking Clinic / mQuit** services; counselling + drug doubles quit rates
cards.m: Ask-Advise-Assess-Assist-Arrange

cards.q: Which tool screens for hazardous alcohol use in primary care, and what follows a positive screen?
cards.a:
• **AUDIT** (10 items; 8 or more = hazardous) or the short **AUDIT-C**
• Positive: **brief intervention** (FRAMES: Feedback, Responsibility, Advice, Menu, Empathy, Self-efficacy)
• Dependence or withdrawal risk: refer for supervised detoxification
cards.m: AUDIT the drinker, then FRAME the advice

cards.q: Which CV risk score does the Malaysian CVD prevention CPG use for a man without known CVD, and what are the bands?
cards.a:
• **Framingham General CVD risk score** (10-year risk)
• **Low < 10%**, **intermediate 10-20%**, **high > 20%**
• Diabetes, CKD or established CVD = already high risk, no score needed
cards.m: 10 and 20 split low, medium, high

cards.q: Why do common men's complaints such as ED or LUTS give a KK doctor an opportunity to reduce NCD risk?
cards.a:
• Men rarely attend for prevention but **will attend for sexual or urinary problems**
• ED and LUTS share **DM, HPT, obesity, smoking** risk factors
• Use the visit to check **BP, BMI, glucose, lipids**, smoking and alcohol
cards.m: Treat the complaint, screen the man

cards.q: Define erectile dysfunction (Malaysian CPG 2024).
cards.a:
• **Persistent inability** to **achieve or maintain** an erection
• **Sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance**
• Persistent or recurrent (usually 3 months or more), not an occasional failure
cards.m: Can't Get it or can't Keep it

cards.q: How common is ED in Malaysian men aged 40-79 years?
cards.a:
• About **69.5%** (any degree of ED)
• Prevalence **rises with age** and with DM, HPT and CVD
• So ask about it: most men will not volunteer it
cards.m: About 7 in 10 men over 40

cards.q: What are the three main pathophysiological mechanisms of ED?
cards.a:
• **Vascular insufficiency** (arterial inflow, venous leak)
• **Endothelial dysfunction** (reduced nitric oxide)
• **Altered smooth muscle tone** in the corpora cavernosa
• Note: slide says 'distributors'; meant contributors
cards.m: Pipes, lining, muscle

cards.q: Classify the types of ED with examples.
cards.a:
• **Organic**: **vascular** (atherosclerosis), **neurogenic** (DM neuropathy, spinal injury, stroke), **hormonal** (hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia), **anatomical** (Peyronie's)
• **Psychogenic**: psychosocial issues
• **Mixed**: organic + psychosocial (most common in practice)
cards.m: VNHA: Vessels, Nerves, Hormones, Anatomy

cards.q: Which history features point to psychogenic rather than organic ED?
cards.a:
• **Psychogenic**: **sudden onset**, **situational** (fine with masturbation or another partner), **preserved morning/nocturnal erections**, younger man, life stressor
• **Organic**: **gradual, progressive**, consistent in all situations, **loss of morning erections**, vascular risk factors
cards.m: Morning glory present = mind, not machinery

cards.q: Why is ED called a 'marker' of cardiovascular disease?
cards.a:
• Shares **endothelial dysfunction** and atherosclerosis with CAD
• **Penile arteries (1-2 mm)** narrow and cause symptoms before **coronary arteries (3-4 mm)**
• ED **precedes coronary events by about 2-5 years** - screen every man with ED for CV risk
cards.m: Artery-size hypothesis: small pipes block first

cards.q: List lifestyle risk factors for ED on the slides.
cards.a:
• **Unhealthy diet**, **physical inactivity**, **obesity**
• **Smoking**, **alcohol**
• **Recreational drugs**
• **Pornography** (excessive use)
cards.m: The NCD lifestyle list plus porn

cards.q: List comorbidities associated with ED.
cards.a:
• **Diabetes**, **hypertension**, **cardiovascular disease**
• **ESRD**, **obstructive sleep apnoea**
• **Depression and anxiety**
• **CP/CPPS**, **hypogonadism**, **traumatic brain injury**
cards.m: Think metabolic, cardiac, renal, sleep, mood, hormones

cards.q: Which drug classes commonly cause ED?
cards.a:
• **Antihypertensives** (thiazides, beta-blockers)
• **Finasteride** (5-alpha-reductase inhibitor)
• **Antidepressants** (SSRIs) and **antipsychotics** (raise prolactin)
• Review the drug list before adding a PDE5 inhibitor
cards.m: Before you prescribe, check what they're on

cards.q: What are the components of ED diagnosis and assessment?
cards.a:
• **History** (with validated questionnaire)
• **Physical examination**
• **Laboratory investigations**
• **Cardiovascular risk assessment**
• **Advanced work-up** in selected cases
cards.m: History, Exam, Labs, Heart, then Advanced

cards.q: What is the IIEF-5 and how is it scored?
cards.a:
• **5-item** version of the **International Index of Erectile Function** (also called SHIM)
• Covers confidence, erection for penetration, maintenance, completion, satisfaction over the **past 6 months**
• Each item **1-5**, total **5-25**; lower score = worse ED
• Also used to **monitor treatment response**
cards.m: 5 questions, 5 points each, max 25

cards.q: Give the IIEF-5 severity bands.
cards.a:
• **22-25**: no ED
• **17-21**: mild
• **12-16**: mild to moderate
• **8-11**: moderate
• **5-7**: severe
cards.m: 22, 17, 12, 8, 5 - each band steps down about 5

cards.q: What does the Erection Hardness Score (EHS) grade?
cards.a:
• **Penile rigidity**, single question, grades **0-4**
• 1 = larger but not hard; 2 = hard but **not enough for penetration**
• 3 = hard enough for penetration but not completely hard; 4 = **completely hard, fully rigid**
cards.m: Tofu, peeled banana, unpeeled banana, cucumber

cards.q: What should be examined in a man presenting with ED?
cards.a:
• **Genitourinary**: penis (Peyronie's plaque, phimosis), testes (size - hypogonadism)
• **Vascular**: peripheral pulses
• **Endocrine**: secondary sexual characteristics, gynaecomastia
• **Neurological**: perineal sensation, reflexes
• **BP, HR, BMI, waist circumference**
cards.m: Genitals, vessels, glands, nerves, vitals

cards.q: Which laboratory tests are done for ED?
cards.a:
• **FBG / HbA1c** and **lipid profile** (vascular risk)
• **Early morning total testosterone**
• **Total PSA** (if age-appropriate or before testosterone therapy)
• **Prolactin, LH** if testosterone is low
cards.m: Sugar, fat, testosterone; then prolactin and LH if low

cards.q: Why must testosterone be measured in the early morning?
cards.a:
• Testosterone has a **diurnal rhythm** - peaks **7-11 am**
• A low result should be **repeated** before diagnosing hypogonadism
• Low testosterone + **high LH** = primary (testicular); low/normal LH = secondary (check prolactin)
cards.m: Catch testosterone at its morning high

cards.q: Name the advanced ED work-up tests and the key use of NPTR.
cards.a:
• **Nocturnal penile tumescence and rigidity (NPTR) test**
• **Intracavernosal injection test** (vascular integrity)
• **Penile arteriography** (before revascularisation)
• NPTR: **normal nocturnal erections suggest psychogenic ED**
cards.m: Sleep tells the truth

cards.q: Which domains are covered in the psychological and sexual assessment of ED?
cards.a:
• **Current psychological state** (anxiety, depression)
• **Relationship** and **partner's sexual functioning**
• **Life stressors** and coping
• **Cognitive factors** (performance anxiety)
• **Sexual factors** and **co-morbid sexual dysfunction** (premature ejaculation)
cards.m: Mind, partner, stress, thoughts, other dysfunctions

cards.q: A man has both ED and premature ejaculation. Which is treated first?
cards.a:
• **Treat the ED first** (PDE5 inhibitor)
• PE is often **secondary to ED** - men rush to ejaculate before losing the erection
• Reassess PE once erections improve
cards.m: Fix the erection, the hurry often fixes itself

cards.q: Princeton III: what are the low, intermediate and high cardiac risk categories for sexual activity?
cards.a:
• **Low**: asymptomatic, < 3 risk factors, controlled HTN, mild stable angina, NYHA I-II - **treat ED, may resume sex**
• **Intermediate**: 3 or more risk factors, moderate angina, MI 2-8 weeks ago, NYHA III - **cardiac evaluation (stress test) first**
• **High**: unstable angina, uncontrolled HTN, NYHA IV, MI < 2 weeks, high-risk arrhythmia, severe aortic stenosis - **defer sex, refer cardiology**
cards.m: Green go, amber test, red stop

cards.q: How can you judge at the bedside whether a man with heart disease is fit for sexual activity?
cards.a:
• Sexual intercourse needs about **3-5 METs**
• If he can do **4 METs** - e.g. **climb two flights of stairs briskly** or walk 1.6 km in 20 min - **without symptoms**, risk is low
• If not, arrange an exercise stress test
cards.m: Two flights of stairs = fit for the bedroom

cards.q: Outline the biopsychosocial management of ED in primary care.
cards.a:
• **Biological**: **PDE5 inhibitors**, **vacuum erection device**, **treat underlying disease** (DM, HPT)
• **Psychological**: counselling, psychotherapy, sex therapy
• **Social**: **lifestyle and risk factor modification**
• Refer to **urology** if initial primary-care treatment fails
cards.m: Body, mind, life

cards.q: Which lifestyle changes improve erectile function?
cards.a:
• **Physical activity** (aerobic exercise)
• **Diet and weight loss**
• **Smoking and alcohol cessation**
• Also improve CV risk - win-win
cards.m: What's good for the heart is good for the penis

cards.q: How do PDE5 inhibitors work?
cards.a:
• Sexual stimulation releases **nitric oxide** → raises **cGMP** → smooth-muscle relaxation → erection
• **PDE5** breaks down cGMP; inhibitors **prolong cGMP action**
• So they **need sexual stimulation** - they are not aphrodisiacs and do not cause spontaneous erections
cards.m: PDE5i turns up the volume, but stimulation must play the music

cards.q: Compare the initial dose, onset and duration of sildenafil, tadalafil and avanafil.
cards.a:
• **Sildenafil**: **50 mg**, onset **30-60 min**, lasts up to **about 4 h**
• **Tadalafil**: **10 mg**, onset **about 30 min**, lasts **36 h**
• **Avanafil**: **100 mg**, onset **< 15 min**, lasts **> 6 h**
cards.m: Tadalafil = 'the weekender' (36 h); avanafil = the fastest

cards.q: What are the side effects of PDE5 inhibitors, and why do sildenafil and tadalafil differ?
cards.a:
• **Headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion** (vasodilatation)
• **Visual abnormalities** - blue tinge with sildenafil (cross-inhibits retinal **PDE6**)
• **Myalgia and back pain** - mainly tadalafil (cross-inhibits **PDE11** in muscle)
• Rare: NAION (sudden visual loss), priapism
cards.m: Sildenafil sees blue; tadalafil has a sore back

cards.q: What is the absolute contraindication to PDE5 inhibitors and why?
cards.a:
• **Any nitrate** (GTN, isosorbide mononitrate/dinitrate, amyl nitrite 'poppers') and **nicorandil**; also riociguat
• Both raise cGMP → **profound, refractory hypotension**, MI, death
• No nitrate for **24 h after sildenafil/avanafil** or **48 h after tadalafil** - tell the ED team
cards.m: Nitrate + PDE5i = blood pressure falls off a cliff

cards.q: How should a patient be counselled to take sildenafil versus tadalafil?
cards.a:
• **Sildenafil**: take **about 1 h before** sex on an **empty stomach** - a **heavy/fatty meal delays** absorption
• **Tadalafil**: **food does not matter**; on-demand or **daily 5 mg** (also helps BPH-LUTS)
• Both **need sexual stimulation** to work
cards.m: Sildenafil hates a big dinner

cards.q: A man says sildenafil 'did not work'. What must you check before calling it a treatment failure?
cards.a:
• **Correct use**: timing, food, **sexual stimulation**, enough **attempts (at least 4-6)**
• **Dose titrated** to maximum (sildenafil 100 mg)
• Uncorrected **hypogonadism**, poor DM control, relationship or psychological issues
• Then switch PDE5i or refer to urology
cards.m: Most 'failures' are really 'mis-use'

cards.q: Why is caution needed when a PDE5 inhibitor is combined with an alpha-blocker?
cards.a:
• Both are vasodilators → **additive postural hypotension**
• Patient should be **stable on the alpha-blocker first**, then start the PDE5i at the **lowest dose**
• Not an absolute contraindication (unlike nitrates)
cards.m: Alpha + PDE5 = dizzy when standing

cards.q: How does a vacuum erection device (VED) work and what are its cautions?
cards.a:
• Cylinder creates **negative pressure** → blood drawn into penis; **constriction ring** at the base keeps it
• Ring off within **30 min** (ischaemia)
• Caution with **bleeding disorders / anticoagulants**
• Useful when PDE5i are contraindicated (e.g. on nitrates)
cards.m: Pump it in, ring it, remove within 30

cards.q: What are the second-line pharmacological options for ED and the key complication?
cards.a:
• **Intracavernosal injection** (alprostadil, PGE1) - works without stimulation
• **Intraurethral alprostadil** pellet
• Complication: **priapism** - erection **> 4 h is an emergency** (risk of fibrosis)
• Usually started by urology
cards.m: Needle or pellet when the pill fails

cards.q: What are the surgical options for ED?
cards.a:
• **Penile revascularisation surgery** - young men with **isolated arterial lesion** after pelvic/perineal trauma
• **Penile prosthesis** (malleable or inflatable) - for failure of other treatments
• Both by urology
cards.m: Re-plumb the young, implant the rest

cards.q: When should a man with ED be referred to secondary care?
cards.a:
• **Failure of primary-care treatment** (PDE5i used correctly)
• **Urological concern** after evaluation (Peyronie's, testicular or prostate abnormality)
• **Underlying medical conditions** needing specialist care (endocrine, cardiac high risk)
• **Significant psychological factors** (psychiatry / sex therapy)
cards.m: Fail, Find, Fragile, Feelings

cards.q: Define infertility and state when to assess a couple earlier.
cards.a:
• **Failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months** of **regular unprotected intercourse**
• Assess **after 6 months** if the **female partner is 35 or older** or there are **significant risk factors** (e.g. known male factor, cryptorchidism, chemotherapy)
cards.m: 12 months, or 6 if she is 35

cards.q: How common is infertility and how often is a male factor involved?
cards.a:
• Affects about **1 in 6 people** of reproductive age worldwide (WHO 2023)
• **Male factor** contributes in about **half** of infertile couples (sole cause in about 20-30%)
• So **always assess both partners** - semen analysis early
cards.m: It takes two: investigate him too

cards.q: Classify the causes of male infertility.
cards.a:
• **Pre-testicular**: hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia, **anabolic steroids**
• **Testicular**: **varicocele**, **cryptorchidism**, mumps orchitis, Klinefelter syndrome, chemo/radiation, torsion
• **Post-testicular**: obstruction (**CBAVD**, vasectomy, infection), ejaculatory dysfunction
• About a third are **idiopathic**
cards.m: Before, in, after the testis

cards.q: What medical history is relevant in male infertility?
cards.a:
• **Systemic disease**: DM, HPT (and their drugs)
• **Infections**: **STIs** (epididymitis, obstruction), mumps, febrile illness or URTI (fever suppresses spermatogenesis for about 3 months)
• **Family history** of infertility
cards.m: Sugar, pressure, infections, family

cards.q: What reproductive and sexual history should you take from the male partner?
cards.a:
• **Partner's age**, duration of trying, **contraceptive method** and duration
• **Previous pregnancy / miscarriage** with any partner
• **Previous fertility treatment**
• **Libido, potency, ejaculation** (and coital frequency/timing)
cards.m: Who, how long, ever before, and does it work

cards.q: Which gonadotoxin exposures impair spermatogenesis?
cards.a:
• **Chemicals**: pesticides, **organic solvents**, **heavy metals** (lead)
• **Chemotherapy** agents
• **Radiation**
• Also heat (saunas, laptops, prolonged sitting)
• Offer **sperm banking** before chemo/radiotherapy
cards.m: Pesticide, solvent, metal, chemo, rays

cards.q: Which childhood, developmental and surgical history matters in male infertility?
cards.a:
• **Cryptorchidism** (undescended testis), **hernia**, **torsion**
• **Puberty onset** (delayed = hypogonadism)
• Surgery: **orchidopexy, herniorrhaphy** (vas injury), **prostatectomy**
cards.m: Groin history = fertility history

cards.q: Which lifestyle factors reduce male fertility, and why are anabolic steroids important?
cards.a:
• **Obesity**, poor diet, **smoking**, **alcohol**, recreational drugs
• **Anabolic steroids / testosterone**: negative feedback suppresses **LH and FSH** → **oligo- or azoospermia**
• Often reversible over months after stopping
cards.m: Gym testosterone switches off the sperm factory

cards.q: What general and penile findings are sought on examination of an infertile man?
cards.a:
• **General**: **poor virilisation**, **gynaecomastia**, **BMI**
• **Penis**: **hypospadias, epispadias, phimosis, curvature** (affect sperm deposition)
• Inguinal/genital **scars** (previous surgery)
cards.m: Look at the man, then the penis, then the scars

cards.q: How are the testes examined in male infertility and what do small testes suggest?
cards.a:
• Assess **location, size, consistency**, pain, nodules, tenderness
• Volume by **orchidometer**: normal adult about **15-25 mL**
• **Small testes** (under about 12-15 mL) suggest **primary testicular failure**
• **Small, firm testes** are classic of **Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)**
cards.m: Size reflects sperm production

cards.q: What is the significance of an impalpable vas deferens?
cards.a:
• Suggests **congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD)** → **obstructive azoospermia** with low semen volume
• Strongly linked to **CFTR (cystic fibrosis) mutations** - offer CF testing to both partners
• Also feel the epididymis for obstruction or inflammation
cards.m: No vas? Think CF

cards.q: Describe a varicocele and how to examine for it.
cards.a:
• Dilated **pampiniform venous plexus** - 'bag of worms'
• About **90% left-sided** (left testicular vein drains at right angle into left renal vein)
• Examine **standing** and with **Valsalva**
• Sudden right-sided or non-reducing varicocele: exclude **renal/retroperitoneal mass**
cards.m: Bag of worms on the left; on the right think renal tumour

cards.q: How should a semen sample be collected?
cards.a:
• **2-7 days of sexual abstinence**
• **Masturbation** into a **sterile wide-mouthed container** (no ordinary condom - spermicidal)
• **Complete sample**, kept at **body temperature**, delivered to lab **within 1 h**
cards.m: 2-7 days off, all of it, warm, within the hour

cards.q: What are the WHO (6th edition, 2021) lower reference limits for semen analysis?
cards.a:
• **Volume 1.4 mL**
• **Concentration 16 million/mL**; **total count 39 million** per ejaculate
• **Total motility 42%**; **progressive motility 30%**
• **Vitality 54%**; **normal morphology 4%**
• Older WHO 2010 values: 1.5 mL, 15 million/mL

cards.q: Semen analysis is abnormal. What is the next step and why?
cards.a:
• **Repeat the semen analysis**, ideally **after about 3 months**
• Spermatogenesis takes about **74 days** (~3 months), and one sample varies with illness, fever, abstinence
• Repeat **sooner** if gross abnormality (azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia)
cards.m: Sperm are made over 3 months, so wait 3 months

cards.q: Define oligozoospermia, asthenozoospermia, teratozoospermia and azoospermia.
cards.a:
• **Oligozoospermia**: low sperm **count/concentration**
• **Asthenozoospermia**: low **motility**
• **Teratozoospermia**: abnormal **morphology**
• **Azoospermia**: **no sperm** in the ejaculate (centrifuged sample)
• Combined defects = OAT syndrome
cards.m: Oligo = few, astheno = weak, terato = monster, a- = none

cards.q: How is azoospermia worked up and managed from primary care?
cards.a:
• Repeat to confirm; check **FSH, LH, testosterone** (± prolactin)
• **High FSH + small testes** = non-obstructive (testicular failure) → **karyotype**, Y-chromosome microdeletion
• **Normal FSH + normal testes** = likely obstructive (check vas, CFTR)
• **Refer** to urology / fertility centre (surgical sperm retrieval, ICSI)
cards.m: FSH high = factory failed; FSH normal = pipes blocked

cards.q: What contraceptive methods are available to men?
cards.a:
• **Male condom** - only male method that also **protects against STIs/HIV**
• **Withdrawal** (coitus interruptus) - high failure (about 20% typical use)
• **Vasectomy** - permanent
• **Hormonal male contraception** (testosterone + progestogen) - still **experimental**, not available
cards.m: Condom, Coitus interruptus, Cut

cards.q: What counselling points make male condom use effective?
cards.a:
• Use **from the start** of every act, **new condom each time**
• Check expiry, squeeze tip to expel air, withdraw while erect holding the rim
• **Water-based lubricant only** with latex (oil-based products weaken latex)
• Failure about **2% perfect use vs 13% typical use**; know about **emergency contraception**
cards.m: Oil breaks latex

cards.q: What must a man be told about when a vasectomy becomes effective?
cards.a:
• **Not immediately effective** - sperm remain in the distal vas
• **Post-vasectomy semen analysis** at about **12 weeks** (and at least 20 ejaculations)
• **Continue other contraception** until **azoospermia is confirmed**
• Permanent (reversal unreliable); does **not** affect testosterone, libido or erections; late failure about 1 in 2000
cards.m: Snip, then 12 weeks and a clear sample before going bare

cards.q: Define lower urinary tract symptoms and give their prevalence in Malaysian men.
cards.a:
• A range of symptoms from conditions affecting the **bladder, prostate and urethra**
• **42.7%** of Malaysian men have **moderate-to-severe LUTS**
• Prevalence **rises with age**
• LUTS is a symptom complex, **not a diagnosis**
cards.m: LUTS describes; it doesn't diagnose

cards.q: Using 'FUNSDISH', separate storage from voiding LUTS.
cards.a:
• **Storage (irritative) - FUNS**: **F**requency, **U**rgency (± urge incontinence), **N**octuria, **S**uprapubic pain
• **Voiding (obstructive) - DISH**: post-micturition **D**ribble, **I**ncomplete emptying, **S**training / weak **S**tream, **H**esitancy
cards.m: FUNS = bladder irritated; DISH = outflow obstructed

cards.q: Storage-predominant vs voiding-predominant LUTS: what conditions does each suggest?
cards.a:
• **Storage (irritative)**: **UTI**, **bladder stones**, **bladder tumour** (also overactive bladder, DM polyuria)
• **Voiding (obstructive)**: **BPH**, **prostate cancer**, **urethral stricture**
• Note: slide p32 mislabels voiding as '(Storage)'; correct label is voiding (obstructive)
cards.m: Irritated lining vs blocked outlet

cards.q: List the risk factors for LUTS in men.
cards.a:
• **Increasing age**
• **Obesity / metabolic syndrome**
• **Smoking**, **alcohol**
• **Sedentary lifestyle**
• **Medications** (anticholinergics, decongestants, beta-agonists, TCAs, diuretics)
cards.m: Same NCD lifestyle list plus drugs

cards.q: Which drugs worsen LUTS and by what mechanism?
cards.a:
• **Anticholinergics** and **TCAs**: weaken detrusor → **retention**
• **Decongestants** (pseudoephedrine) and **beta-agonists/sympathomimetics**: raise bladder-neck tone → retention
• **Diuretics**: increase urine volume → **frequency, nocturia**
cards.m: Cold-and-flu tablets can tip an old prostate into retention

cards.q: Which associated symptoms must be asked about in a man with LUTS?
cards.a:
• **Dysuria** and **fever** (UTI, prostatitis)
• **Haematuria** (stone, tumour)
• **Flank pain** (stone, hydronephrosis)
• Plus duration, onset and whether **progressive or intermittent**
cards.m: Burn, fever, blood, flank

cards.q: What are the red flags in a man with LUTS?
cards.a:
• **Haematuria**
• **Incontinence, especially at night** (overflow from chronic retention)
• **Urinary retention**
• **Recurrent UTI**, **bladder calculus**
• **Renal impairment**, **hydronephrosis**
cards.m: Blood, wet bed, can't pass, keeps infecting, stones, kidneys

cards.q: Which medical conditions in the history suggest a non-prostatic cause of LUTS?
cards.a:
• **Diabetes** (polyuria, neuropathic bladder)
• **Neurological**: **stroke**, **Parkinson's disease**, **multiple sclerosis**, spinal disease
• **Renal disease**, previous **UTI**
• Also HPT/hyperlipidaemia (and their diuretics)
cards.m: Sugar and nerves can mimic a prostate

cards.q: Which quality-of-life domains should you ask about in LUTS, and why do they matter?
cards.a:
• **Sleep** (nocturia), **work productivity**, **sexual function**, **emotional well-being**
• **Bother**, not just symptom count, drives treatment
• Social history: **fluid intake, caffeine, alcohol, smoking, exercise**
cards.m: Treat the bother, not the number

cards.q: What are the four parts of the physical examination in male LUTS?
cards.a:
• **Abdomen**: suprapubic area for **distended bladder**
• **External genitalia & perineum**: urethral discharge, **meatal stenosis**, **phimosis**, penile lesions
• **DRE**: prostate size, consistency, tenderness (exclude malignancy)
• **Neurological**: lower limbs, **anal tone, saddle sensation**
cards.m: Belly, bits, bottom, nerves

cards.q: Why is the neurological examination part of LUTS assessment?
cards.a:
• Assess **lower limbs, anal tone and saddle sensation**
• Excludes **neurogenic bladder** (spinal cord lesion, **cauda equina**, MS, Parkinson's, diabetic neuropathy)
• New retention + saddle anaesthesia + reduced anal tone = **emergency MRI/referral**
cards.m: Saddle numb + can't pee = cauda equina until proven otherwise

cards.q: List the primary-care investigations for male LUTS.
cards.a:
• **Urinalysis**
• **Ultrasound KUB / prostate** (± post-void residual)
• **Bladder diary / frequency-volume chart**
• **Renal profile** (urea, creatinine, eGFR)
• **Fasting blood glucose**
• **PSA** (after counselling)
cards.m: Urine, Ultrasound, Urine diary, Urea, sUgar, PSA

cards.q: What does urinalysis screen for in a man with LUTS?
cards.a:
• **UTI** (leucocytes, nitrites) - send culture if positive
• **Haematuria** - stone, tumour, infection; needs further work-up
• **Glycosuria** - undiagnosed **diabetes** causing frequency and nocturia
cards.m: Bugs, blood, sugar

cards.q: When is a bladder diary (frequency-volume chart) used and what can it reveal?
cards.a:
• Record **time and volume** of every void for **2-3 days**
• Use when there is **daytime frequency** or **nocturia of 2 or more** voids a night
• Reveals **nocturnal polyuria** (over **one-third** of 24-h output at night in older men), global polyuria, or small fixed bladder capacity
cards.m: Measure before you medicate the bladder

cards.q: What do the renal profile and ultrasound KUB add in male LUTS?
cards.a:
• **Renal profile**: urea, creatinine, eGFR - **renal impairment from obstruction**
• **Ultrasound KUB/prostate**: **hydronephrosis**, bladder wall thickening/diverticula, stones, **prostate volume**, post-void residual
• Raised creatinine or hydronephrosis = **refer**
cards.m: Is the back-pressure reaching the kidneys?

cards.q: Describe the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS).
cards.a:
• **7 symptom questions**: incomplete emptying, frequency, intermittency, urgency, weak stream, straining, nocturia
• Each scored **0-5** → total **0-35**
• Plus a separate **quality-of-life (bother) question** scored **0-6**
• Used for severity, treatment choice and follow-up
cards.m: 7 questions x 5 = 35

cards.q: Give the IPSS severity bands and the linked management.
cards.a:
• **Mild 0-7**: **watchful waiting** + lifestyle advice
• **Moderate 8-19**: drug therapy usually offered (alpha-blocker ± 5-ARI)
• **Severe 20-35**: drug therapy and consider **urology referral**
cards.m: 7 and 19 are the cut points

cards.q: What do uroflowmetry and post-void residual (PVR) volume tell you?
cards.a:
• **Uroflowmetry**: **Qmax < 10 mL/s** suggests bladder outlet obstruction (needs voided volume over 150 mL)
• **PVR** by bladder ultrasound: large or rising residual (e.g. over 200-300 mL) = **chronic retention** risk
• High PVR = **avoid antimuscarinics**, consider referral
cards.m: Slow flow + big residual = blocked outlet

cards.q: Define benign prostatic hyperplasia and state where it arises.
cards.a:
• **Non-malignant proliferation** of **smooth muscle and epithelial (stromal-epithelial) cells**
• Arises in the **transition zone** (around the urethra)
• Constricts the urethra → **LUTS**
• Contrast: prostate **cancer** mostly arises in the **peripheral zone** (felt on DRE)
cards.m: BPH = Transition (inside); Cancer = Peripheral (outside)

cards.q: At what age does BPH start and how common is it?
cards.a:
• Can start from **age 40**; **common from 50** onwards
• Histological BPH in about **50% of men at 60** and up to **90% by 85**
• Not all enlarged prostates cause symptoms
cards.m: Half of men at 60, nearly all by 85

cards.q: Why does the prostate enlarge with age (hormonal basis)?
cards.a:
• **Testosterone** is converted to **dihydrotestosterone (DHT)** by **5-alpha-reductase** in the prostate
• DHT drives **stromal and epithelial growth**
• Needs functioning testes - men castrated before puberty do not develop BPH
• Basis for **5-alpha-reductase inhibitor** treatment
cards.m: No DHT, no BPH

cards.q: List the risk factors for BPH.
cards.a:
• **Age** and **genetic predisposition**
• **Diabetes mellitus**, **obesity**, **hyperlipidaemia**, **hypertension** (metabolic syndrome)
• **Diet**: pro-inflammatory, high protein, low fruit and vegetables
• **Localised (prostatic) inflammation**
cards.m: Old genes + metabolic syndrome + bad diet + inflammation

cards.q: What symptoms does BPH cause?
cards.a:
• **Storage**: frequency, urgency, nocturia
• **Voiding**: hesitancy, weak stream, straining, dribbling
• **Complications**: acute or chronic retention, UTI, urinary calculi, **overflow incontinence**
• Severity and QoL impact measured with **IPSS**
cards.m: Both FUNS and DISH, then complications

cards.q: Contrast acute and chronic urinary retention in BPH.
cards.a:
• **Acute**: sudden inability to void, **painful**, tense tender bladder; often triggered by drugs, constipation, alcohol, UTI → **catheterise**
• **Chronic**: **painless**, large residual, **overflow incontinence** (often nocturnal enuresis), risk of **hydronephrosis and renal failure**
• High-pressure chronic retention: watch for **post-obstructive diuresis** after catheterisation
cards.m: Acute aches; chronic creeps up silently

cards.q: What are the complications of BPH?
cards.a:
• **Acute urinary retention**
• **Chronic retention** → **obstructive uropathy / renal impairment**
• **Recurrent UTI**, **bladder stones**, bladder diverticula
• **Haematuria** (fragile prostatic veins)
• **Overflow incontinence**
cards.m: Stuck, Stones, Sepsis, Sore kidneys, Spotting blood

cards.q: What does the prostate feel like on DRE in BPH compared with prostate cancer?
cards.a:
• **BPH**: **enlarged, smooth, rubbery/firm, symmetrical, non-tender**, **median sulcus preserved**, no blood on the glove
• **Cancer**: **hard, irregular/nodular**, asymmetrical, **loss of median sulcus**
• **Prostatitis**: **tender**, boggy, warm
cards.m: BPH = smooth like the tip of your nose; cancer = hard like your knuckle

cards.q: Which investigations are listed for suspected BPH?
cards.a:
• **UFEME** and **urine C&S**
• **Renal profile**
• **Serum PSA** (after counselling; helps estimate prostate volume and cancer risk)
• **Uroflowmetry**
• **Ultrasound KUB & prostate** (volume, hydronephrosis, PVR)
cards.m: Urine x2, kidneys, PSA, flow, scan

cards.q: Which men with BPH are suitable for watchful waiting?
cards.a:
• **Mild symptoms (IPSS 7 or less)**, or moderate symptoms with **little bother**
• **No complications** (no retention, recurrent UTI, stones, haematuria, renal impairment)
• Lifestyle advice + **review annually** (repeat IPSS)
cards.m: Low score, low bother, no complications = watch

cards.q: List the non-pharmacological (lifestyle) measures for BPH-LUTS.
cards.a:
• **Reduce fluid intake** before going out or sleeping (but not below about 1.5 L/day)
• **Reduce caffeine and alcohol**
• **Avoid drugs that worsen LUTS** (diuretics timing, decongestants, antidepressants)
• **Bladder training**; **pelvic floor exercises**
• **Treat and prevent constipation**
cards.m: Fluids, caffeine, drugs, bladder, pelvic floor, bowels

cards.q: How do alpha-1 blockers work in BPH and which are used?
cards.a:
• Block alpha-1 receptors in **prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle** → relaxation → better flow (the **dynamic** component)
• **Tamsulosin 400 micrograms OD** (uroselective), **terazosin**, doxazosin, alfuzosin
• Terazosin: start **1 mg at night**, titrate (usual 2-10 mg). Note: slide gives 2-8 mg ON
cards.m: Alpha-blockers relax the squeeze; they don't shrink the gland

cards.q: What are the key side effects of alpha-blockers?
cards.a:
• **Postural hypotension**, dizziness, **first-dose syncope** (non-selective: terazosin, doxazosin) → **take at night**
• **Abnormal / retrograde ejaculation** (tamsulosin)
• **Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome** → tell the **ophthalmologist before cataract surgery**
• Nasal congestion, asthenia
cards.m: Dizzy, Dry ejaculation, Droopy iris

cards.q: Alpha-blocker vs 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor: which works faster?
cards.a:
• **Alpha-blocker**: works in **days to a few weeks** - first choice for **bothersome moderate-severe LUTS**
• **5-ARI**: needs **3-6 months** (up to 12) for full effect as the gland shrinks
• Warn patients on 5-ARI not to stop early
cards.m: Alpha is the sprinter, 5-ARI the marathon runner

cards.q: How do 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors work and who benefits?
cards.a:
• **Finasteride 5 mg OD**, **dutasteride 0.5 mg OD** - block conversion of testosterone to **DHT**
• **Shrink prostate volume** by about 20-30% (the **static** component)
• Best for **enlarged prostate** (over 30-40 mL or PSA over 1.5 ng/mL)
• **Reduce risk of acute retention and need for surgery**
cards.m: Finasteride Fattens nothing: it shrinks

cards.q: What are the side effects of 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors?
cards.a:
• **Reduced libido**, **erectile dysfunction**, ejaculatory disorders
• **Gynaecomastia** / breast tenderness
• **Lowers PSA by about 50%**
• Teratogenic: women who are or may become pregnant should not handle crushed tablets
cards.m: Shrinks the prostate - and sometimes the sex drive

cards.q: How should PSA be interpreted in a man on finasteride or dutasteride?
cards.a:
• 5-ARIs **reduce PSA by about 50%** after **6-12 months**
• **Double the measured PSA** to estimate the true value
• Any **rise in PSA while on a 5-ARI** is suspicious → evaluate for cancer
• Record a baseline PSA before starting
cards.m: On a 5-ARI, double it

cards.q: When is combination therapy (alpha-blocker + 5-ARI) indicated?
cards.a:
• **Moderate-to-severe LUTS** with an **enlarged prostate** (over 30-40 mL) or raised PSA
• i.e. **high risk of progression** (older, large gland)
• Better than either drug alone for symptom control and preventing retention/surgery
cards.m: Quick relief + long-term shrink

cards.q: How are storage-predominant LUTS treated in a man with BPH?
cards.a:
• Add an **antimuscarinic** (e.g. solifenacin, tolterodine) or **mirabegron** (beta-3 agonist)
• **Check post-void residual first** - avoid if large residual (retention risk)
• Antimuscarinic caution in the elderly (**cognitive impairment**, dry mouth, constipation)
cards.m: Check the residual before you relax the bladder

cards.q: Which PDE5 inhibitor treats both BPH-LUTS and ED?
cards.a:
• **Tadalafil 5 mg once daily**
• Improves LUTS (relaxes prostate/bladder smooth muscle) and erections
• Same **nitrate contraindication**; caution with alpha-blockers (hypotension)
cards.m: One tablet, two problems

cards.q: When should a man with BPH be referred to urology for surgery (e.g. TURP)?
cards.a:
• **Refractory or recurrent urinary retention**
• **Recurrent UTI**, **recurrent haematuria**, **bladder stones**
• **Renal impairment / hydronephrosis** due to obstruction
• **Failed or poorly tolerated medical therapy**, severe bothersome symptoms
• **Suspicious DRE or PSA** (exclude cancer)
cards.m: Retain, Recur, Renal, Refractory, Rule out cancer

cards.q: Primary-care management of acute urinary retention in a man with BPH?
cards.a:
• **Urethral catheterisation** (suprapubic if urethral fails or prostatitis suspected); record **drained volume**
• Look for precipitants: drugs, constipation, UTI, alcohol
• **Start an alpha-blocker** before **trial without catheter (TWOC)** - improves success
• Refer to urology
cards.m: Drain, find the trigger, alpha-block, then trial off

cards.q: What is prostatitis and whom does it typically affect?
cards.a:
• A group of conditions with **voiding discomfort** and **pain** in the prostate referred to the **perineum, low back, urethra and testes**
• Typically men aged **25-50 years** (younger than BPH)
cards.m: Young man with perineal pain - think prostate

cards.q: Give the NIH classification of prostatitis.
cards.a:
• **I**: acute bacterial prostatitis (about 5%)
• **II**: chronic bacterial prostatitis
• **III**: **chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome** (IIIA inflammatory, IIIB non-inflammatory) - **about 90%**, most common
• **IV**: asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis (incidental finding)
cards.m: I acute, II chronic bug, III pain without bug, IV found by accident

cards.q: What are the causes and risk factors of acute bacterial prostatitis?
cards.a:
• **Ascending urethral infection** or reflux of infected urine
• **Chronic indwelling catheter**, recent instrumentation/biopsy
• **Diabetes mellitus**, **immunosuppression**
• Young sexually active men: consider **gonorrhoea/chlamydia**
cards.m: Catheter, Diabetes, Immunosuppressed - CDI

cards.q: Which organisms most commonly cause acute bacterial prostatitis?
cards.a:
• **Escherichia coli** (most common)
• **Klebsiella pneumoniae**
• **Enterococcus faecalis**
• **Pseudomonas aeruginosa** (especially after catheter/instrumentation)
cards.m: Same gut Gram-negatives as UTI: E. coli leads

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of acute bacterial prostatitis?
cards.a:
• **Systemic**: **fever, sweating, rigors**
• **Pain**: mainly **perineal**, also back and suprapubic
• **Urinary**: frequency, urgency, **dysuria** ± haematuria
• May present with **acute retention**
cards.m: A UTI with fever and a sore bottom

cards.q: What are the examination findings and investigations in acute bacterial prostatitis?
cards.a:
• **DRE**: prostate **tender, swollen, firm, warm, indurated**
• **CRP** (± FBC, blood cultures if septic)
• **Urine Gram stain and culture** - positive
• NAAT for gonorrhoea/chlamydia in young sexually active men
cards.m: Hot, swollen, exquisitely tender gland

cards.q: Why must vigorous prostatic massage be avoided in acute bacterial prostatitis?
cards.a:
• Extremely painful
• Can push bacteria into the bloodstream → **bacteraemia / sepsis**
• DRE should be **gentle**; diagnose from midstream urine culture
• Prostatic massage (EPS) is only for **chronic** prostatitis
cards.m: Acute: touch gently; chronic: massage

cards.q: How is mild acute bacterial prostatitis treated orally, and why is the course long?
cards.a:
• **Ciprofloxacin 500-750 mg PO BD** for **14 days** (many guidelines: 2-4 weeks)
• Alternative: **co-trimoxazole 160/800 mg PO 12-hourly**
• Long course because antibiotics **penetrate the prostate poorly**; short courses relapse into **chronic bacterial prostatitis**
• Adjust to culture; analgesia, fluids
cards.m: Prostate = antibiotic fortress: lipid-soluble drug, long siege

cards.q: How is severe acute bacterial prostatitis managed?
cards.a:
• **Admit** (septic, unable to tolerate oral, retention, immunosuppressed)
• **IV amoxicillin (ampicillin) 2 g 6-hourly + gentamicin 4-6 mg/kg/day**
• Step down to oral (e.g. ciprofloxacin) to complete 2-4 weeks
• Retention: **suprapubic catheter** preferred
cards.m: Septic prostate = IV amp + gent

cards.q: What are the complications of acute bacterial prostatitis?
cards.a:
• **Prostatic abscess** (suspect if no improvement in 48-72 h → transrectal US/CT)
• **Acute urinary retention**
• **Sepsis / urosepsis**
• Progression to **chronic bacterial prostatitis**, epididymo-orchitis
cards.m: Abscess, Retention, Sepsis, Chronicity

cards.q: What causes chronic bacterial prostatitis?
cards.a:
• **Undertreated acute bacterial prostatitis**
• **Recurrent UTI** with **intraprostatic reflux** of urine
• **Ascending urethral** infection
• **Lymphogenous / haematogenous** spread of rectal bacteria
• Less common than non-bacterial (CP/CPPS)
cards.m: Half-treated acute becomes chronic

cards.q: How does chronic bacterial prostatitis present?
cards.a:
• **Chronic or recurrent urogenital symptoms** lasting **at least 3 months**
• **Recurrent UTIs with the same organism**
• **Pelvic discomfort**, **pain during or after ejaculation**
• Usually **afebrile** between episodes
cards.m: Same bug, again and again, for 3 months

cards.q: How is chronic bacterial prostatitis confirmed?
cards.a:
• **DRE**: normal to **mildly tender** prostate
• **Pre- and post-prostatic massage urine** (2-glass test) or **expressed prostatic secretions (EPS)** (Meares-Stamey 4-glass)
• Post-massage specimen shows **excess white cells** and bacteria at higher counts than pre-massage urine
cards.m: Massage it to find the bug

cards.q: How is chronic bacterial prostatitis treated?
cards.a:
• **Ciprofloxacin 500-750 mg PO BD for 4-6 weeks** (good prostatic penetration)
• Atypicals (Chlamydia, Mycoplasma): **doxycycline 100 mg BD for 10 days** or **azithromycin**. Note: slide says doxycycline 100 mg OD; standard dosing is BD
• **NSAIDs** for pain; **alpha-blockers** if voiding symptoms
cards.m: Chronic = 4-6 weeks of quinolone

cards.q: Define chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS).
cards.a:
• **Chronic pelvic or urogenital/sexual pain or discomfort** for **at least 3 of the previous 6 months**
• **No evidence of active UTI** or identifiable bacterial infection
• The **most common** form of prostatitis (about 90%)
cards.m: Pain 3 of 6 months, no bugs

cards.q: What is the cause of CP/CPPS?
cards.a:
• **Unknown** - probably multifactorial
• **Pelvic floor muscle dysfunction** (spasm, trigger points)
• **Neuropathic pain** / central sensitisation
• **Psychological factors** (stress, anxiety, depression)
cards.m: Muscles, nerves, mind - not microbes

cards.q: How is CP/CPPS diagnosed?
cards.a:
• **Diagnosis of exclusion**
• **DRE**: normal to mildly tender prostate
• Exclude UTI (urine culture), STI, urethral stricture, bladder cancer (haematuria), stones
• **NIH-CPSI** questionnaire scores pain, urinary symptoms and QoL
cards.m: Rule everything else out first

cards.q: How is CP/CPPS managed?
cards.a:
• **Multimodal**: **alpha-blocker** (voiding symptoms), **analgesics** (NSAIDs), **pelvic floor physiotherapy**, **stress management**
• **Antibiotics only** if trialled **early** (one course of 4-6 weeks); do not repeat if no benefit
• **Psychological support**; explain it is not infection or cancer
cards.m: Treat the phenotype, not a phantom bug

cards.q: Why do many men with mental health problems not seek help?
cards.a:
• **Social expectations** of masculinity and **stigma**
• Emotional expression seen as **vulnerability / weakness**
• So men **bottle up** emotions - distress comes from **emotional suppression**, not only depression
cards.m: 'Boys don't cry' keeps men out of clinics

cards.q: List five reasons men are reluctant to seek mental health help.
cards.a:
• **Societal expectations of masculinity**
• **Fear of judgement and shame**
• **Different symptom expression** (missed by self and clinicians)
• **Action-over-words mentality** (fix it alone, don't talk)
• **Lack of awareness or resources**
cards.m: Masculinity, Shame, Masked symptoms, Must act, Missing resources

cards.q: How may depression present differently in men?
cards.a:
• **Irritability, anger, aggression** rather than sadness
• **Alcohol or substance misuse**, **risk-taking**, gambling
• **Overworking**, withdrawal, **somatic complaints** (fatigue, headache, back pain, ED)
• So screen actively; standard criteria may miss 'male depression'
cards.m: Angry, drinking, working late - ask about mood

cards.q: What is the gender paradox in suicide?
cards.a:
• **Women attempt** suicide more often
• **Men die by suicide** about **3-4 times more often** - more lethal methods, less help-seeking, alcohol
• A man with depression, alcohol misuse, recent loss (job, relationship, money) is **high risk**
cards.m: Women attempt, men complete

cards.q: How does men's health-seeking behaviour differ from women's?
cards.a:
• **Lower healthcare utilisation** overall
• **Delay** seeking professional treatment → present later, sicker
• Perceive expressing symptoms or concern as **weak and not masculine**
cards.m: Men come late, if at all

cards.q: How do age and education affect men's help-seeking?
cards.a:
• **Older age** and **higher education level** significantly **increase** the likelihood of seeking treatment
• So **young, less-educated men** are the hardest-to-reach group - target them with outreach
cards.m: Young and less schooled = least likely to come

cards.q: How does conformity to gender norms affect men's help-seeking?
cards.a:
• Seeking medical attention feels like **'killing their pride'**
• Men **conceal their problems** rather than appear weak
• Clinician response: **normalise**, frame help-seeking as **strength and responsibility** to family
cards.m: Pride hides pain

cards.q: How do men's attitudes to treatment affect adherence, and how can you counter it?
cards.a:
• They **doubt therapy** if there is **no quick improvement** → **high default risk**
• Counter: explain **antidepressants take 2-4 weeks** to start working and should continue **at least 6-12 months** after remission
• Arrange **early follow-up** (within 2 weeks) and set clear goals
cards.m: Warn before they quit: slow start is normal

cards.q: How do affordability and accessibility limit men's healthcare use?
cards.a:
• Many men are **breadwinners** → put **health as lowest priority**, cannot take time off work
• Some **live far from health facilities**
• Solutions: **after-hours clinics**, workplace screening, telehealth, bringing services closer
cards.m: No time, no money, too far

cards.q: How can the stigma around men's mental health be broken?
cards.a:
• Message: **'It's okay not to be okay'**
• **National awareness campaigns** (media, social media)
• **Religious leaders** spreading awareness: e.g. **Khutbah Jumaat**, ceramah maghrib
• Men hear it from voices they already trust
cards.m: Mosque and media

cards.q: What early-education strategies does the seminar propose for men's mental health?
cards.a:
• **Men's mental health education** in **preschool, school and universities**
• **Community service** programmes that **cater to all age groups**
• Builds emotional literacy before stigma sets in
cards.m: Teach boys before they become silent men

cards.q: What is first-line drug treatment for moderate depression in a man at a KK, and what side effect commonly causes men to default?
cards.a:
• **SSRI** (e.g. **fluoxetine 20 mg** or **sertraline 50 mg** OD) + psychological therapy (e.g. CBT, problem-solving)
• **Sexual dysfunction** (delayed ejaculation, low libido, ED) - men often stop silently
• **Ask about it** and manage (dose change, switch, e.g. to mirtazapine or bupropion)
cards.m: Ask about sex or he'll stop the SSRI

cards.q: Which tools screen for depression and distress in a Malaysian Klinik Kesihatan?
cards.a:
• **PHQ-2** (quick screen) then **PHQ-9** (severity: 5 mild, 10 moderate, 15 moderately severe, 20 severe)
• **DASS-21** (depression, anxiety, stress) - widely used in KK
• PHQ-9 item 9 (thoughts of self-harm) positive → **assess suicide risk the same day**
cards.m: PHQ-9 steps of 5: 5-10-15-20

cards.q: A man discloses suicidal thoughts. What do you do in the KK?
cards.a:
• **Ask directly** about plans, means, intent - asking **does not increase** risk
• Assess risk factors: male, alcohol, previous attempt, isolation, recent loss
• **Plan or intent** = do not leave alone, **same-day psychiatric referral / ED**
• Remove means, involve family, safety plan
cards.m: Ask, Assess, Act - never leave a high-risk man alone

cards.q: Which Malaysian helplines can be given to a distressed man?
cards.a:
• **Talian HEAL 15555** (MOH psychosocial support line)
• **Befrienders** (24-hour emotional support)
• Plus KK mental health services and psychiatry referral
cards.m: HEAL = 15555

cards.q: Give practical consultation strategies to engage men in mental health care.
cards.a:
• Use **problem-solving, action-oriented** language ('stress', 'burnout', 'performance') rather than 'emotions'
• Ask about mood when men present with **ED, insomnia, alcohol or physical complaints**
• Offer **flexible hours**, brief focused visits, digital follow-up
• Involve family where welcomed
cards.m: Speak the language of action

cards.q: Give the key Malaysian epidemiology of colorectal cancer (NCR 2017-2021).
cards.a:
• **23,871 cases** in 2017-2021 (up from 15,515 in 2012-2016)
• **More common in males (57%)** than females (43%)
• **Most common cancer in males**, 2nd in females
cards.m: CRC is number 1 in Malaysian men

cards.q: Which ethnic group has the highest CRC incidence in Malaysia, and at what stage do most present?
cards.a:
• Highest in **Chinese**, then **Indians**
• Incidence **rises with age**
• About **74%** are diagnosed at **late stage (III or IV)** - hence the need for screening
cards.m: 3 of 4 present too late

cards.q: What are the non-modifiable risk factors for colorectal cancer?
cards.a:
• **Age over 50**
• **Family history** of CRC in a **first-degree relative**
• **Previous colorectal polyps** (adenomas)
• **Hereditary syndromes**: **FAP**, **Lynch syndrome** (HNPCC)
• **Inflammatory bowel disease** (UC, Crohn's colitis)
cards.m: Age, Ancestry, Adenoma, Autosomal syndromes, Angry bowel

cards.q: What are the modifiable risk factors for colorectal cancer?
cards.a:
• **Smoking**
• **Diabetes mellitus**
• **Overweight / obesity**
• **Alcohol**
• **Low-fibre, high-fat diet** (and processed/red meat, inactivity)
cards.m: Same men's NCD risk factors again

cards.q: What are the symptoms of colorectal cancer?
cards.a:
• **Per rectal bleeding**
• **Altered bowel habit**
• **Anaemia**
• **Loss of weight or appetite**
• Abdominal discomfort / constipation
• **Mucoid stool, tenesmus** (rectal)
cards.m: Bleeding, Bowel change, Blood count low, Body weight down

cards.q: Which signs may be found on examination in colorectal cancer?
cards.a:
• **Palpable abdominal mass** (often right iliac fossa caecal tumour)
• **Palpable anorectal mass** on **DRE**
• Pallor; hepatomegaly if liver metastases
• Always do a **DRE** in rectal bleeding or bowel change
cards.m: If you don't put your finger in it, you'll put your foot in it

cards.q: Why must unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in a man always be investigated?
cards.a:
• Men (and post-menopausal women) have **no physiological blood loss**
• IDA = **occult GI bleeding until proven otherwise** - especially **right-sided colon cancer**
• Refer for **colonoscopy (and OGDS)**; do not just give iron
cards.m: Iron-deficient man = scope him

cards.q: How do right-sided and left-sided colon cancers present differently?
cards.a:
• **Right (caecum, ascending)**: **iron deficiency anaemia**, weight loss, RIF mass; bowel habit often normal (liquid stool)
• **Left / rectum**: **rectal bleeding**, **change in bowel habit**, tenesmus, obstruction (narrow lumen, solid stool)
cards.m: Right bleeds silently; left blocks loudly

cards.q: What is the national CRC screening test for average-risk adults in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **Immunochemical faecal occult blood test (iFOBT)**
• Target: **asymptomatic, average-risk** adults aged **50-75 years**
• Available at **Klinik Kesihatan**; immunochemical (detects human haemoglobin) so **no dietary restriction**
cards.m: 50 to 75: iFOBT alive

cards.q: What is the next step after a positive iFOBT?
cards.a:
• **Refer for colonoscopy** - do not simply repeat the iFOBT
• A positive test is not a diagnosis; colonoscopy finds cancer or adenomas (polypectomy)
• Negative iFOBT: **repeat** screening at the programme interval
cards.m: Positive FIT = scope it, never retest it

cards.q: A man has rectal bleeding and weight loss. Should he have an iFOBT?
cards.a:
• **No** - iFOBT is a **screening** test for **asymptomatic** people
• Symptomatic patients with red flags need **direct referral for colonoscopy**
• A negative iFOBT must not falsely reassure
cards.m: Screen the well; scope the symptomatic

cards.q: How should a man with a first-degree relative with CRC be screened?
cards.a:
• **Colonoscopy** (not iFOBT)
• Start at **age 40**, or **10 years before the age** the relative was diagnosed, whichever is earlier
• **FAP / Lynch** families: genetic counselling and much earlier, frequent colonoscopy
cards.m: Family history: 40 or 10 years earlier

cards.q: How is colorectal cancer diagnosed, and what is the role of CEA?
cards.a:
• **Colonoscopy + biopsy (HPE)** confirms diagnosis
• **CEA**: **baseline** and **surveillance** for recurrence
• CEA is **not a screening or diagnostic test** (not sensitive or specific; raised in smokers)
cards.m: Biopsy diagnoses; CEA follows up

cards.q: How is colorectal cancer staged?
cards.a:
• **CT thorax, abdomen and pelvis** - local and distant staging
• **MRI pelvis** - **rectal** cancer local staging
• **Endorectal ultrasound** - early rectal cancer
• **FDG PET-CT** - suspected **recurrence**, not routine initial staging
cards.m: CT for all, MRI for the rectum, PET for relapse

cards.q: How is colorectal cancer treated?
cards.a:
• **Stage-dependent**
• **Surgical resection** (mainstay)
• **Chemotherapy ± radiotherapy** (neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for rectal)
• **Palliative / supportive care**
• **Follow-up and surveillance** (CEA, CT, colonoscopy)
cards.m: Cut, chemo, comfort, check

cards.q: What is the primary-care role in a man treated for colorectal cancer?
cards.a:
• **Support treatment and surveillance** (ensure CEA, CT, colonoscopy done)
• **Manage comorbidities** (DM, HPT)
• **Promote healthy lifestyle**
• **Psychosocial and palliative support**; stoma care
• Screen **first-degree relatives**
cards.m: Support, Surveil, Sugar & pressure, Soul, Siblings

cards.q: Give the key Malaysian epidemiology of lung cancer (NCR 2017-2021).
cards.a:
• **17,028 cases** (up from 11,256 in 2012-2016)
• **More common in males (67.4%)** than females (32.6%)
• **2nd most common cancer in males**, 3rd in females; rises with age
• **95%** diagnosed at **late stage (III-IV)** where staging known
cards.m: Lung: 2nd in men, 95% late

cards.q: What are the risk factors for lung cancer?
cards.a:
• **Lifestyle**: **smoking** (dominant cause)
• **Environmental**: **second-hand smoke**, **radon**, **air pollution**
• **Occupational**: **asbestos**, **diesel exhaust**, **silica** (silicosis)
• **Personal**: increasing **age**, **COPD**, **family history** of lung cancer
cards.m: Smoke, Second-hand, Site (work), Self (age, COPD, family)

cards.q: What are the symptoms of lung cancer?
cards.a:
• **Prolonged, unresolved cough**
• **Haemoptysis** / rust-coloured sputum
• **Chest pain**, **dyspnoea**
• **Unexplained weight loss / loss of appetite**
• **Hoarseness** (recurrent laryngeal nerve)
• **Recurrent chest infections** (obstructed bronchus)
cards.m: Cough that won't quit in a man who won't quit

cards.q: Which findings in a smoker over 40 should prompt an urgent chest X-ray?
cards.a:
• **Haemoptysis** (unexplained - most urgent)
• **Cough or change in cough over 3 weeks**, unexplained dyspnoea, chest pain
• **Weight loss, appetite loss**, fatigue
• **Finger clubbing**, **supraclavicular lymphadenopathy**, persistent chest signs
• **Chest infection not resolving** or recurring
cards.m: Blood, 3 weeks of cough, clubbing, nodes

cards.q: Who is eligible for lung cancer screening according to the slides?
cards.a:
• Age **45-75 years** with a **20-year or longer smoking history** (current or former smokers)
• **High-risk non-smokers over 40** with significant **family history** (first-degree relative)
• Many guidelines express the smoking threshold as **20 pack-years** (USPSTF: 50-80 years, quit within 15 years)
cards.m: 45-75, 20 years of smoke

cards.q: What is the recommended lung cancer screening test, and why not a chest X-ray?
cards.a:
• **Low-dose CT (LDCT) thorax** - gold standard
• LDCT screening reduced lung cancer mortality by about **20%** in the NLST trial
• **CXR screening does not reduce mortality** - misses small early tumours
• CXR is for **symptomatic** patients
cards.m: Screen with CT, investigate symptoms with CXR

cards.q: What harms should be discussed before LDCT lung screening?
cards.a:
• **False positives** (benign nodules) → anxiety, further scans, biopsies
• **Overdiagnosis** of indolent cancers
• **Radiation** (cumulative), **incidental findings**
• Requires **shared decision-making** and must be combined with **smoking cessation** - screening is not a licence to smoke
cards.m: Screening finds things - not all of them matter

cards.q: Describe the primary-care referral pathway for suspected lung cancer.
cards.a:
• Signs/symptoms suggestive of lung cancer → **chest X-ray**
• Assess **clinical suspicion + CXR findings**
• **CXR abnormal** OR **high clinical suspicion despite a normal CXR** → **urgent referral to a lung specialist**
• Further assessment ± **CT scan**
cards.m: Abnormal film or worried mind → refer

cards.q: Does a normal chest X-ray exclude lung cancer in a symptomatic smoker?
cards.a:
• **No** - CXR can miss central, small or retrocardiac tumours (sensitivity about 75-80%)
• **Persistent haemoptysis** or **high clinical suspicion** → **urgent referral** even with a normal CXR
• Specialist arranges **CT thorax** ± bronchoscopy
cards.m: Treat the patient, not the film

cards.q: How is lung cancer managed in hospital?
cards.a:
• Treatment guided by **histology** (small-cell vs non-small-cell) and **stage**
• **Surgical resection** for early-stage NSCLC
• **Neoadjuvant / peri-operative therapy** where indicated
• **Adjuvant therapy** by stage and **tumour biomarkers** (EGFR, ALK, PD-L1)
• Specialist surveillance
cards.m: Histology + stage + biomarkers decide

cards.q: What is the primary-care role in lung cancer?
cards.a:
• **Identify risk factors**, particularly **smoking**
• **Smoking cessation** and risk-reduction counselling
• **Early recognition** of signs and symptoms
• **Arrange CXR** for suspected cases
• **Timely referral** to a lung specialist
cards.m: Identify, Quit, Recognise, X-ray, Refer

cards.q: Which oncological emergencies and paraneoplastic syndromes can lung cancer cause?
cards.a:
• **Superior vena cava obstruction**: facial swelling, distended neck veins, dyspnoea
• **Hypercalcaemia** (PTHrP - squamous cell): confusion, polyuria, constipation
• **SIADH** (small-cell): hyponatraemia
• **Spinal cord compression** from metastases; Horner's/Pancoast (apical tumour)
cards.m: Squamous = Stones (calcium); Small cell = Sodium low

cards.q: Give the key Malaysian epidemiology of prostate cancer (NCR 2017-2021).
cards.a:
• **6,441 cases** (up from 4,189 in 2012-2016)
• **3rd most common cancer** in Malaysian males
• Incidence rises markedly with age, **especially from 50**
• **63.3%** diagnosed at **late stage (III-IV)**
cards.m: Prostate: 3rd in men, 2 in 3 late

cards.q: What are the risk factors for prostate cancer?
cards.a:
• **Increasing age** - particularly over 50
• **Family history** of prostate cancer (first-degree relative)
• **Genetic predisposition** - **BRCA1/BRCA2** mutations (BRCA2 strongest)
• **Ethnicity** - higher risk in men of **African ancestry**
cards.m: Age, Ancestry, African, BRCA

cards.q: How does prostate cancer present?
cards.a:
• **Often asymptomatic** in early stage (peripheral zone, away from urethra)
• **LUTS** (frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak stream) - usually from coexisting BPH or locally advanced disease
• **Haematuria**, **urinary retention / obstruction**
• **Bone pain** - suggests **metastatic** disease
cards.m: Early is silent; bone pain means spread

cards.q: Why is new back pain with leg weakness in a man with prostate cancer an emergency?
cards.a:
• Prostate cancer metastasises to **bone (vertebrae)** → risk of **metastatic spinal cord compression**
• Red flags: back pain, **leg weakness, sensory level, urinary retention, bowel dysfunction**
• **Same-day referral**, urgent **MRI whole spine**, **high-dose dexamethasone**, radiotherapy/surgery
cards.m: Back pain + prostate cancer = MRI today

cards.q: What DRE findings suggest prostate cancer?
cards.a:
• **Hard / firm** prostate
• **Irregular or nodular** surface
• **Loss of the median sulcus** (asymmetry, local spread)
• **Any abnormal DRE = refer**, whatever the PSA
cards.m: Hard, Lumpy, Lost groove

cards.q: Why can DRE detect prostate cancer but not most BPH changes?
cards.a:
• About **70% of prostate cancers** arise in the **peripheral zone** - posterior, felt through the rectum
• **BPH** arises in the **transition zone** (central) - felt only as smooth symmetrical enlargement
• Anterior and small tumours are missed, so DRE and PSA complement each other
cards.m: Cancer lives at the back door

cards.q: What is PSA and why is it an imperfect cancer test?
cards.a:
• **Prostate-specific antigen** - a serine protease made by prostatic epithelium
• **Organ-specific, not cancer-specific**: raised by BPH, prostatitis, UTI, retention
• Common cut-off **4 ng/mL**, but about 15% of men with PSA below 4 still have cancer
• Use **age-specific ranges** and trends
cards.m: Prostate-specific, not cancer-specific

cards.q: List the causes of a raised PSA other than prostate cancer.
cards.a:
• **BPH** (larger gland)
• **UTI** and **prostatitis**
• **Urinary retention**, **catheterisation**, cystoscopy, **prostate biopsy**
• **Recent ejaculation**, vigorous exercise (cycling)
• **Increasing age**
cards.m: BPH, Bugs, Blocked, Bladder tubes, Biopsy, Bedroom, Bicycle

cards.q: When should a PSA test be deferred to avoid a false-positive result?
cards.a:
• **6 weeks** after a **UTI / prostatitis** (treat first, then retest)
• **6 weeks** after **prostate biopsy**
• **48 hours** after **ejaculation** or **vigorous exercise**
• About **1 week** after DRE (minor effect)
• Urinary retention / recent catheter: defer
cards.m: Infection 6 weeks, sex 2 days

cards.q: What must a man be told before a PSA test (shared decision-making)?
cards.a:
• **Benefit**: may detect cancer early and modestly reduce prostate cancer death
• **Harms**: **false positives** → anxiety, **biopsy** (bleeding, sepsis); **overdiagnosis** of slow cancers; treatment side effects (**incontinence, ED**)
• A normal PSA does not fully exclude cancer
• Decision is **his**, after balanced information
cards.m: Inform, don't just test

cards.q: Which men should be offered informed PSA testing?
cards.a:
• Well-informed men from about **age 50** with over 10-15 years' life expectancy
• **Earlier (about 45)** if **high risk**: first-degree relative with prostate cancer, **African ancestry**, (from 40 if **BRCA2** carrier)
• Not for men with short life expectancy
• Symptomatic men: PSA as part of **diagnostic** work-up, not screening
cards.m: 50 for most, 45 if family or African, 40 if BRCA2

cards.q: When should a man be referred urgently to urology for suspected prostate cancer?
cards.a:
• **Abnormal DRE** (hard, nodular, asymmetrical) - **regardless of PSA**
• **Raised PSA** above the age-specific reference (repeat after excluding UTI if appropriate)
• **Bone pain or symptoms of metastases** with raised PSA
• Rising PSA on a **5-ARI**
cards.m: Hard prostate or high PSA → urology

cards.q: What is the diagnostic pathway for suspected prostate cancer?
cards.a:
• **Serum PSA** (+ DRE)
• **Multiparametric MRI prostate** (mpMRI) - before biopsy, targets lesions
• **Prostate biopsy** (TRUS-guided or **transperineal**, lower sepsis risk) → **histopathology**
• **Grading**: ISUP Grade Group / Gleason score
• **Staging imaging** according to risk (bone scan, PSMA PET, CT)
cards.m: PSA → MRI → Biopsy → Grade → Stage

cards.q: Explain the Gleason score and ISUP Grade Group.
cards.a:
• **Gleason**: sum of the two most common architectural patterns (each 3-5), e.g. **3+4 = 7**
• **ISUP Grade Group 1-5**: GG1 = Gleason 6; GG2 = 3+4; GG3 = 4+3; GG4 = 8; GG5 = 9-10
• Higher grade = more aggressive; guides surveillance vs treatment
cards.m: GG1 low, GG5 high

cards.q: How is localised prostate cancer managed?
cards.a:
• **Active surveillance** - **selected low-risk** patients (PSA, MRI, repeat biopsy; treat if progression)
• **Radical prostatectomy**
• **Radiotherapy** (external beam ± ADT, brachytherapy)
• Side effects of radical treatment: **urinary incontinence, ED**, bowel symptoms (RT)
cards.m: Watch, cut, or radiate

cards.q: How is advanced prostate cancer treated and what should primary care monitor?
cards.a:
• **Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT)**-based systemic therapy ± androgen receptor pathway inhibitor or chemotherapy
• **Supportive and palliative care**
• Monitor **PSA**, disease progression, and **ADT side effects**: hot flushes, **osteoporosis**, **diabetes/weight gain**, **CV risk**, ED, fatigue, depression
cards.m: ADT starves the cancer - and the bones and heart

cards.q: Which conditions make a focus on men's health screening worthwhile?
cards.a:
• **Cardiovascular disease** (leading male killer)
• **Colorectal cancer** (most common male cancer)
• **Lung cancer**
• All share **preventable risk factors** and are **detectable early**
cards.m: Heart, bowel, lungs

cards.q: What are the common risk factors that men often ignore or leave undiagnosed?
cards.a:
• **Hypertension**
• **Diabetes mellitus**
• **Poor lifestyle habits**: **smoking**, **excessive alcohol**, **lack of exercise**
• Hidden behind **masculinity norms, poor healthcare utilisation, different symptom expression, fear of judgement**
cards.m: Silent pressure, silent sugar, loud habits

cards.q: What personal reasons stop men going for health check-ups?
cards.a:
• **Fear of being diagnosed**
• **Do not think they are at risk** ('I feel fine')
• Plus pride, cost, and time off work
cards.m: 'What I don't know can't hurt me'

cards.q: What health-system reasons stop men attending check-ups?
cards.a:
• **Complicated processes** (queues, forms, appointments)
• **Lack of doctor recommendation**
• **Healthcare not male-friendly** (opening hours clash with work, female-oriented clinics)
cards.m: Hard to get in, nobody asked, not built for men

cards.q: What are the proven benefits of screening men?
cards.a:
• Early screening **reduces deaths** from **cardiovascular disease** and **colorectal cancer**
• Detects **treatable men's health issues** - **erectile dysfunction**, **premature ejaculation**
• ED found at screening may reveal hidden CVD/DM
cards.m: Screening saves hearts and bowels - and sex lives

cards.q: How does health-screening uptake compare between Malaysian men and women?
cards.a:
• **Women 60.8% vs men 53.8%** (NHMS 2023)
• Despite many programmes, **low uptake** persists and the **NCD burden remains high**
cards.m: About 54% of men vs 61% of women

cards.q: What strategies can improve men's uptake of health screening?
cards.a:
• Develop **male-specific health promotion** programmes
• **Bring screening closer to men** - workplaces, mosques, community events, after-hours
• **Use digitalisation** (online booking, reminders, apps, telehealth)
• Doctors actively **recommend** screening at every contact
cards.m: Target, take it to them, tech

cards.q: Name Malaysian government programmes supporting NCD screening.
cards.a:
• **KOSPEN** (Komuniti Sihat Pembina Negara) - community volunteers screen BP, glucose, BMI
• **PeKa B40** - free health screening for **B40 adults aged 40 and above** (and spouses)
• **NHSI** (National Health Screening Initiative)
• **BSSK** (Borang Saringan Status Kesihatan) used in KK
cards.m: KOSPEN in the kampung, PeKa for B40

cards.q: What should a routine health screen of a 50-year-old man at a KK include?
cards.a:
• **BP, BMI, waist circumference**
• **Fasting glucose / HbA1c**, **lipid profile**, renal function → **CV risk score**
• **Smoking** (offer cessation), **alcohol** (AUDIT), **mood** (PHQ/DASS)
• **iFOBT** (50-75); PSA only after counselling; LDCT if eligible smoker
• Ask about **ED and LUTS**, sexual health/HIV risk, vaccinations
cards.m: Numbers, habits, mood, cancers, below the belt

cards.q: Why is ED a useful 'entry point' for screening men?
cards.a:
• Men will seek help for sexual problems when they avoid general check-ups
• ED predicts **CVD by 2-5 years** and may reveal **undiagnosed DM, HPT, dyslipidaemia, hypogonadism, depression**
• Every ED consult = full **CV risk assessment**
cards.m: Come for the erection, leave with a check-up

cards.q: What does Surah Al-Isra (17:36) teach about health?
cards.a:
• 'Indeed, the **hearing, sight and intellect** - all will be called to account'
• Our senses and mind are **entrusted** to us - we are answerable for how we use and protect them
• So **listen to warnings** and **use your eyes and mind**
cards.m: Hearing, sight, heart - all accountable

cards.q: How does the Aqli-Naqli message apply to men's health-seeking?
cards.a:
• The body is an **amanah (trust)** from Allah - caring for it is a duty
• **Stop guessing, stop avoiding check-ups** - get screened
• Staying healthy **protects your family** (men as providers)
cards.m: Health is a trust, not a private matter

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man who has worked in a granite quarry for 25 years attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 years of progressive exertional breathlessness and dry cough. He has never smoked. Chest X-ray shows multiple small nodular opacities in both upper zones and eggshell calcification of the hilar lymph nodes.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Silicosis
Asbestosis
Pulmonary tuberculosis
Sarcoidosis
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
mcq.e: Quarrying exposes workers to crystalline silica dust; silicosis gives upper-zone nodules and the classic eggshell calcification of hilar nodes. Asbestosis is a lower-zone fibrosis with pleural plaques. Always take an occupational history - men dominate dusty occupations, and silicosis also raises the risk of TB and lung cancer.
w: Correct - silica exposure + upper-zone nodules + eggshell hilar calcification is classic.
Wrong - asbestosis causes lower-zone reticular fibrosis and pleural plaques, after asbestos (not granite) exposure.
Wrong - TB can complicate silicosis but does not cause eggshell nodal calcification; there is no fever or weight loss.
Wrong - sarcoidosis gives bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in younger adults, without the occupational link.
Wrong - this follows organic antigen exposure (birds, mouldy hay), not mineral dust.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old taxi driver is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan for hypertension follow-up. He drinks 4-5 cans of beer most evenings. His AUDIT score is 14. He has no tremor, morning drinking or previous withdrawal symptoms. GGT is mildly raised.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer for admission and supervised inpatient detoxification
Start disulfiram once he has been abstinent for 24 hours
Reassure him because the score is below the dependence range
Give a structured brief intervention and arrange follow-up
Start oral naltrexone and review liver function in a month
mcq.e: An AUDIT score of 8-15 indicates hazardous drinking, for which a brief intervention (feedback, advice, goal-setting) in primary care is effective. Detoxification and anti-craving drugs are for dependence (scores of 20 or more, or withdrawal features). Reassurance misses the chance to prevent liver disease, a disease driven mainly by alcohol in Malaysian men.
w: Wrong - there are no features of dependence or withdrawal, so inpatient detox is unnecessary.
Wrong - disulfiram is for motivated dependent drinkers aiming at abstinence, not first-line for hazardous use.
Wrong - an AUDIT of 8 or more is hazardous drinking and needs intervention, not reassurance.
Correct - AUDIT 8-15 = hazardous drinking; brief intervention with follow-up is the evidence-based step.
Wrong - pharmacotherapy is reserved for alcohol dependence, not hazardous drinking alone.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan health screen. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and has no diabetes or known CVD. BP is 152/94 mmHg on repeated readings; total cholesterol 6.4 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L. His Framingham 10-year general CVD risk is calculated at 26%.
Which management best matches his risk category?
o: Low risk: lifestyle advice and repeat the risk score in five years
High risk: lifestyle measures plus statin and antihypertensive drugs
Intermediate risk: lifestyle measures and repeat lipids in one year
Intermediate risk: start antihypertensives but defer statins for now
Low risk: smoking cessation alone, as BP and lipids are borderline
mcq.e: The Malaysian CVD prevention CPG grades Framingham 10-year risk as low (under 10%), intermediate (10-20%) and high (over 20%). At 26% he is high risk and needs drug treatment of BP and lipids in addition to lifestyle change, including smoking cessation. The trap is treating each factor as 'borderline' when together they put him above 20%.
w: Wrong - 26% is not low risk (under 10%).
Correct - over 20% is high risk; treat BP and lipids with drugs alongside lifestyle change.
Wrong - intermediate is 10-20%; he is above this.
Wrong - he is not intermediate, and statins should not be deferred at high risk.
Wrong - smoking cessation is vital but BP 152/94 and his total risk need drug treatment.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old man who smokes 20 cigarettes a day is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan for a sprained ankle. When advised to stop smoking, he says he enjoys smoking and is not ready to quit in the next month.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Prescribe varenicline and set a quit date within the next week
Refer him to the Quit Smoking Clinic and close the topic for now
Avoid discussing it further until he raises the subject himself
Advise switching to e-cigarettes as a safer long-term alternative
Use a motivational (5 R's) discussion and offer to revisit it
mcq.e: For smokers not ready to quit, the recommended approach is a motivational intervention using the 5 R's: Relevance, Risks, Rewards, Roadblocks and Repetition. Prescribing or setting a quit date before he is ready usually fails. Each contact should repeat the offer of help, because readiness changes over time.
w: Wrong - pharmacotherapy and a quit date are for smokers who are ready to quit.
Wrong - referral is unlikely to be taken up while he is unmotivated; motivational work comes first.
Wrong - missing the opportunity is poor practice; brief advice should be given at every contact.
Wrong - e-cigarettes are not recommended as a cessation strategy in Malaysian guidance.
