Correct - 5 R's motivational interviewing is the step for the smoker not yet ready to quit.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old office manager attends a Klinik Kesihatan for the first time in 6 years with a sore throat. His father had a myocardial infarction at 50. He smokes and has a BMI of 29 kg/m2. BP today is 144/92 mmHg.
What is the best approach at this visit?
o: Treat the sore throat and advise him to return if he feels unwell
Refer him to cardiology for an exercise stress test this month
Start low-dose aspirin for primary prevention of heart disease
Treat the sore throat and screen glucose, lipids, BP and CV risk
Arrange a yearly resting ECG as his main cardiac screening test
mcq.e: Men use health services less (53.8% vs 60.8% screening uptake) and IHD is their leading cause of death, so any visit is a chance for opportunistic NCD screening. He has several risk factors and needs repeat BP, glucose, lipids and a CV risk score. Aspirin is not used for primary prevention, and stress tests or routine ECGs are not screening tools for asymptomatic men.
w: Wrong - waiting for symptoms misses the chance to screen a man who rarely attends.
Wrong - an asymptomatic man does not need a stress test; risk assessment comes first.
Wrong - aspirin is not recommended for primary prevention in such patients (bleeding outweighs benefit).
Correct - opportunistic screening and CV risk assessment target men's under-use of services.
Wrong - routine ECG is not an effective screening test in asymptomatic men.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old engineer attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 months of difficulty maintaining erections with his wife. It began suddenly after a stressful job change. He still wakes with firm morning erections and has normal erections during masturbation. He has no medical illness; examination is normal.
What is the most likely type of erectile dysfunction?
o: Psychogenic erectile dysfunction
Vasculogenic erectile dysfunction
Hypogonadism-related dysfunction
Venous leak (veno-occlusive) dysfunction
Neurogenic erectile dysfunction
mcq.e: Sudden onset, situational ED with preserved morning and masturbatory erections points to a psychogenic cause - the vascular and neural pathways clearly work. Organic ED is gradual, consistent in all situations and loses nocturnal erections. Manage with counselling and addressing stressors, though a PDE5 inhibitor may help confidence.
w: Correct - sudden, situational ED with preserved morning erections is psychogenic.
Wrong - vascular ED is gradual and global, with loss of morning erections and risk factors.
Wrong - hypogonadism causes low libido and reduced morning erections, not situational loss.
Wrong - venous leak gives poor maintenance in all situations, including morning erections.
Wrong - neurogenic ED (DM, spinal injury) is persistent and affects nocturnal erections.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes completes the IIEF-5 questionnaire at a Klinik Kesihatan. His total score is 14.
How is his erectile function graded?
o: No erectile dysfunction
Mild erectile dysfunction
Mild-moderate ED
Moderate erectile dysfunction
Severe erectile dysfunction
mcq.e: IIEF-5 bands: 22-25 no ED, 17-21 mild, 12-16 mild to moderate, 8-11 moderate and 5-7 severe. A score of 14 sits in the 12-16 band. Using the score at baseline lets you measure response to treatment later.
w: Wrong - no ED is 22-25.
Wrong - mild ED is 17-21.
Correct - 12-16 is mild to moderate ED.
Wrong - moderate ED is 8-11.
Wrong - severe ED is 5-7.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old man with stable angina takes isosorbide mononitrate 30 mg daily, amlodipine and atorvastatin. He asks the Klinik Kesihatan doctor for 'the blue pill' for erectile difficulty. His angina has been stable for a year.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Prescribe sildenafil 25 mg and advise him to take it at bedtime
Prescribe tadalafil but keep doses 48 hours apart from his nitrate
Prescribe avanafil, as its short action avoids interaction issues
Avoid PDE5 inhibitors and offer a vacuum erection device instead
Prescribe sildenafil and tell him to omit the nitrate on that day
mcq.e: Regular nitrates (and nicorandil) are an absolute contraindication to every PDE5 inhibitor, because both raise cGMP and can cause profound, refractory hypotension. Dose separation or skipping a long-acting nitrate dose is unsafe. A vacuum erection device, or urology referral for intracavernosal therapy, are appropriate alternatives; any change to anti-anginal drugs is a cardiology decision.
w: Wrong - a low dose does not remove the dangerous nitrate interaction.
Wrong - with a daily long-acting nitrate there is no safe gap; tadalafil lasts 36 h.
Wrong - all PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil, are contraindicated with nitrates.
Correct - nitrates absolutely contraindicate PDE5i; VED is a safe primary-care option.
Wrong - omitting one dose of a long-acting nitrate does not make co-use safe.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old man asks for treatment of erectile dysfunction. He has diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and smokes, but has no chest pain. He is sedentary and has never had cardiac testing. BP is 138/84 mmHg; ECG at rest is normal.
According to the Princeton consensus, what is the best next step before he resumes sexual activity?
o: Reassure him he is low risk and start a PDE5 inhibitor today
Arrange an exercise stress test to stratify his cardiac risk
Advise him to avoid sexual activity until he sees a cardiologist
Start a PDE5 inhibitor together with sublingual GTN as needed
Prescribe a beta-blocker first to protect him during intercourse
mcq.e: Princeton III classes men with three or more CV risk factors as intermediate (indeterminate) risk; they should have further evaluation, usually exercise stress testing, before sexual activity is resumed and ED treated. Low risk is fewer than three risk factors and asymptomatic; high risk includes unstable angina or uncontrolled hypertension. GTN must never be combined with a PDE5 inhibitor.
w: Wrong - four risk factors make him intermediate, not low, risk.
Correct - intermediate risk needs exercise testing to restratify before sex and ED therapy.
Wrong - deferral pending cardiology is for high-risk patients (unstable angina, recent MI, NYHA IV).
Wrong - nitrates are absolutely contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors.
Wrong - a beta-blocker is not a substitute for risk stratification and can worsen ED.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old man with known ischaemic heart disease asks for erectile dysfunction treatment. Over the past 2 weeks his chest pain has come on with less effort and twice occurred at rest. BP is 150/90 mmHg and pulse 88/min.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start tadalafil 5 mg daily and review in four weeks
Arrange an outpatient exercise stress test in a month
Prescribe a vacuum erection device and review symptoms
Start sildenafil 25 mg as he has normal blood pressure
Defer sexual activity and refer urgently to cardiology
mcq.e: Crescendo and rest angina is unstable angina - a high-risk Princeton category in which sexual activity must be deferred and the cardiac condition stabilised first. This man needs urgent cardiology review (possibly emergency department), not ED treatment. Elective stress testing is unsafe in unstable angina.
w: Wrong - ED treatment is deferred in high-risk unstable angina.
Wrong - a stress test is contraindicated in unstable angina, and a month's wait is unsafe.
Wrong - the problem is his unstable heart, not the choice of ED device.
Wrong - BP is not the issue; unstable angina makes any sexual activity unsafe now.
Correct - high-risk (unstable angina): defer sex and refer urgently to stabilise the heart.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man with no known illness attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 6 months of gradually worsening erectile dysfunction. He smokes and has a waist circumference of 102 cm. The doctor checks his BP, fasting glucose and lipids and calculates his CV risk.
What is the main reason for this cardiovascular assessment?
o: Penile arteries are narrower, so atherosclerosis causes ED before angina
PDE5 inhibitors raise coronary risk, so a baseline is needed before use
Sexual intercourse is the main trigger of heart attacks in men with ED
Low testosterone causes ED and directly ruptures coronary artery plaque
Most ED is caused by antihypertensive drugs, which must be identified
mcq.e: ED and coronary artery disease share endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerosis. Because penile arteries (1-2 mm) are smaller than coronary arteries (3-4 mm), the same plaque burden causes symptoms there first - ED precedes coronary events by about 2-5 years. Every man with ED should therefore have a CV risk assessment.
w: Correct - the artery-size hypothesis: ED is an early marker of systemic vascular disease.
Wrong - PDE5 inhibitors do not increase cardiac events (except with nitrates).
Wrong - sexual activity is a rare MI trigger; this is not the reason for screening.
Wrong - hypogonadism is one cause of ED but does not directly cause plaque rupture.
Wrong - drugs are one cause, and he takes none; the vascular link is the key reason.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man was given sildenafil 50 mg two weeks ago. He reports it 'did not work' on both occasions. He took it straight after a large nasi briyani dinner and expected an erection without foreplay. He has well-controlled diabetes; BP 128/80 mmHg.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Switch him to tadalafil because sildenafil has clearly failed
Refer to urology for intracavernosal injection therapy
Check serum testosterone before any further PDE5i trial
Counsel on correct use and retry for at least 4-6 attempts
Increase the dose to 100 mg and take it with the next meal
mcq.e: Most apparent PDE5 inhibitor failures are due to incorrect use. Sildenafil should be taken about an hour before sex on an empty stomach (fatty meals delay absorption) and needs sexual stimulation to work. Treatment failure is only declared after at least 4-6 correct attempts at an adequate dose.
w: Wrong - two incorrect attempts do not count as failure of sildenafil.
Wrong - second-line referral is premature before correct PDE5i use.
Wrong - testosterone may be checked if hypogonadism is suspected, but misuse is the obvious problem here.
Correct - correct timing, empty stomach and sexual stimulation, with enough attempts, come first.
Wrong - taking it with a meal repeats the error; dose increase comes after correct use.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 months of reduced libido and new erectile difficulty. Three months ago he started a new tablet for prostate enlargement. His other medicines - amlodipine, metformin and atorvastatin - are unchanged for 5 years.
Which drug is the most likely cause?
o: Amlodipine
Finasteride
Metformin
Atorvastatin
Paracetamol
mcq.e: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride lower DHT and commonly cause reduced libido, erectile dysfunction and ejaculatory problems. The timing - onset soon after starting the new prostate drug - points to it. Amlodipine is largely neutral for erectile function, unlike thiazides and beta-blockers.
w: Wrong - calcium-channel blockers are relatively ED-neutral and the dose is long-standing.
Correct - finasteride lowers DHT, causing low libido and ED, with a matching time course.
Wrong - metformin does not cause ED and has been taken for years.
Wrong - statins are not a recognised common cause and are long-standing.
Wrong - paracetamol is not a prostate drug and does not cause ED.

mcq.stem:
A 47-year-old man reports erectile dysfunction, reduced libido, tiredness and needing to shave less often. He has a BMI of 33 kg/m2. Testes are small and soft on examination.
Which is the most appropriate initial investigation for his hormonal status?
o: Random afternoon total testosterone
Penile duplex Doppler ultrasound
Serum prolactin as the only hormone test
Nocturnal penile tumescence testing
Early morning (before 11 am) total testosterone
mcq.e: Symptoms of hypogonadism with small testes call for a total testosterone level taken in the morning, when levels peak; an afternoon value may be falsely low. A low result is repeated and then LH and prolactin are checked to separate primary from secondary causes. Doppler and nocturnal tumescence tests assess vascular and psychogenic causes, not hormones.
w: Wrong - testosterone falls through the day, so an afternoon sample may be falsely low.
Wrong - Doppler assesses penile blood flow, not hormonal status.
Wrong - prolactin is checked if testosterone is low, not as the only first test.
Wrong - NPTR distinguishes psychogenic from organic ED; it does not assess hormones.
Correct - morning total testosterone, repeated if low, is the first hormonal test.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man with mild erectile dysfunction says he and his wife dislike having to plan intercourse around a tablet. They prefer a medicine taken on Friday that would still work over the weekend. He has no cardiac disease and takes no nitrates.
Which drug best fits his preference?
o: Sildenafil 50 mg
Avanafil 100 mg
Tadalafil 10 mg
Intraurethral alprostadil
Intracavernosal alprostadil
mcq.e: Tadalafil has a duration of action of about 36 hours, allowing spontaneity over a weekend. Sildenafil lasts about 4 hours and avanafil about 6 hours, though avanafil has the fastest onset. Alprostadil preparations are second-line and act only for one episode.
w: Wrong - sildenafil acts for only about 4 hours.
Wrong - avanafil has the fastest onset but lasts only about 6 hours.
Correct - tadalafil's 36-hour action allows a 'weekend' window.
Wrong - intraurethral alprostadil is second-line and works for one episode only.
Wrong - injections are second-line and do not give a long window of action.

mcq.stem:
A 67-year-old man has taken doxazosin 4 mg nightly for BPH for a year without dizziness. He now requests treatment for erectile dysfunction. BP is 132/78 mmHg with no postural drop. He has no cardiac disease and takes no nitrates.
What is the most appropriate prescribing approach?
o: Start sildenafil at a low dose and warn about postural dizziness
Decline treatment, as alpha-blockers absolutely contraindicate PDE5i
Stop doxazosin so that full-dose sildenafil can be used safely
Start sildenafil 100 mg, as his blood pressure is well controlled
Advise him to take sildenafil and doxazosin together at bedtime
mcq.e: Alpha-blockers and PDE5 inhibitors are both vasodilators, so combining them can cause symptomatic postural hypotension. The combination is allowed (unlike nitrates) if the patient is stable on the alpha-blocker, and the PDE5 inhibitor is started at the lowest dose. Stopping his BPH treatment is unnecessary.
w: Correct - stable on the alpha-blocker, so start a low-dose PDE5i with counselling.
Wrong - this is a caution, not an absolute contraindication (that applies to nitrates).
Wrong - stopping effective BPH treatment is unnecessary; low-dose PDE5i is safe.
Wrong - starting at the maximum dose increases the risk of hypotension.
Wrong - taking both at the same time maximises additive hypotension.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old man reports complete erectile failure for a year after a minor pelvic injury at work. History suggests significant anxiety, and he is making a compensation claim. Examination and blood tests are normal. The urologist wants an objective test of whether his erectile mechanism works during sleep.
Which investigation is most appropriate?
o: Penile duplex Doppler ultrasound
Pelvic angiography (arteriography)
Intracavernosal injection test
Nocturnal penile tumescence and rigidity test
Dynamic infusion cavernosometry
mcq.e: The nocturnal penile tumescence and rigidity (NPTR) test records erections during sleep; normal nocturnal erections indicate an intact organic mechanism and point to psychogenic ED. Doppler and intracavernosal injection tests assess vascular function, and arteriography is reserved for planning revascularisation.
w: Wrong - Doppler assesses arterial inflow and venous leak, not sleep erections.
Wrong - arteriography is used before revascularisation surgery, not to separate psychogenic ED.
Wrong - the injection test checks vascular response to a drug, not natural nocturnal erections.
Correct - NPTR shows whether spontaneous sleep erections occur, separating psychogenic from organic ED.
Wrong - cavernosometry investigates veno-occlusive dysfunction in specialist settings.

mcq.stem:
A 41-year-old man using intracavernosal alprostadil telephones a Klinik Kesihatan. His erection has lasted 5 hours despite ejaculation and is now painful.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Apply cold packs at home and attend the next routine clinic
Take an extra dose of oral analgesia and wait another 6 hours
Attend the emergency department now for urgent decompression
Book a urology clinic appointment for later in the week
Reassure him that it will settle on its own within 24 hours
mcq.e: An erection lasting more than 4 hours is priapism, a urological emergency. Ischaemic priapism after intracavernosal injection needs urgent corporal aspiration and/or an alpha-agonist to prevent irreversible cavernosal fibrosis and permanent ED. Delay of any kind worsens the outcome.
w: Wrong - home measures with delay risk permanent fibrosis.
Wrong - waiting longer prolongs ischaemia.
Correct - priapism over 4 hours needs same-day emergency decompression.
Wrong - an outpatient appointment is far too late.
Wrong - ischaemic priapism does not reliably resolve and causes permanent damage.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man reports ejaculating within a minute of penetration and also losing his erection on several occasions over the past year. He is anxious about both problems. IIEF-5 score is 15. He takes no regular medicines.
What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Daily SSRI for the premature ejaculation alone
Topical lidocaine spray applied before intercourse
Sex therapy targeted at ejaculatory control only
On-demand dapoxetine before intercourse
A PDE5 inhibitor to treat the erectile dysfunction
mcq.e: When ED and premature ejaculation coexist, ED should be treated first. Men often hurry to ejaculate for fear of losing the erection, so PE frequently improves once erections are reliable. Reassess and treat any remaining PE afterwards.
w: Wrong - treating PE first leaves the underlying ED, which often drives the PE.
Wrong - topical anaesthetics may worsen erection quality and do not address ED.
Wrong - ejaculatory techniques alone ignore the erectile problem.
Wrong - dapoxetine targets PE only and is not first when ED coexists.
Correct - treat ED first; secondary PE often resolves as erections improve.

mcq.stem:
A couple attends a Klinik Kesihatan because they have not conceived after 7 months of regular unprotected intercourse. The wife is 36 years old with regular cycles; the husband is 38 and well. Neither has had previous children.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure them and review if not pregnant after 12 months
Begin assessment of both partners, including semen analysis
Refer the couple directly for in-vitro fertilisation
Investigate the wife only, as her age is the main concern
Advise timed intercourse and review again in six months
mcq.e: Infertility is defined as no pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse, but assessment should start after 6 months when the woman is 35 or older or there are risk factors. Male factors contribute in about half of couples, so both partners are assessed, starting with a semen analysis. Direct IVF referral skips basic investigation.
w: Wrong - waiting 12 months is inappropriate when the female partner is 35 or older.
Correct - assess both partners now because she is over 35 and they have tried over 6 months.
Wrong - basic assessment comes before assisted reproduction.
Wrong - male factor contributes in about half, so the husband must also be assessed.
Wrong - further delay is inappropriate given her age.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old man and his 29-year-old wife have not conceived after 14 months of regular unprotected intercourse. His semen analysis at a Klinik Kesihatan shows volume 2.5 mL, concentration 10 million/mL and progressive motility 28%. He had dengue fever with a high fever 5 weeks before the test. Examination is normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer now for intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI)
Start clomiphene to boost his sperm production
Repeat the semen analysis after about 3 months
Arrange scrotal ultrasound and testicular biopsy
Tell him he is sterile and discuss adoption
mcq.e: A single abnormal semen analysis is never enough to diagnose male factor infertility, because results vary widely and are depressed by fever for weeks. Spermatogenesis takes about 74 days, so the test is repeated after about 3 months (sooner only for azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia). His concentration (WHO lower limit 16 million/mL) and progressive motility (30%) are only mildly low.
w: Wrong - assisted reproduction is premature before confirming the abnormality on a repeat test.
Wrong - clomiphene is not first-line and should not be started on one abnormal result.
Correct - repeat after about 3 months (one sperm cycle), especially after a febrile illness.
Wrong - testicular biopsy is a specialist procedure for azoospermia, not mild oligozoospermia.
Wrong - mild abnormalities on one sample do not mean sterility.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old bodybuilder and his 25-year-old wife have not conceived after 14 months. He has injected 'steroids' bought at his gym for 2 years. He has acne, and both testes are small and soft. Two semen analyses show no sperm. LH and FSH are low and serum testosterone is high.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Start testosterone gel to replace the injections he uses
Refer now for surgical sperm retrieval and ICSI treatment
Increase the testosterone dose to restore sperm output
Arrange karyotyping as the first step to find a cause
Stop the steroids and repeat the semen test in 3-6 months
mcq.e: Exogenous androgens suppress pituitary LH and FSH by negative feedback, so intratesticular testosterone falls and spermatogenesis stops, giving small testes and azoospermia with low gonadotrophins. The first step is to stop all androgens; sperm production usually recovers over months (sometimes up to a year or more, and specialists may use hCG). Any form of testosterone, including gel, worsens the problem.
w: Wrong - testosterone gel suppresses LH and FSH just like the injections.
Wrong - this is likely reversible; invasive retrieval is premature.
Wrong - more testosterone deepens the suppression of spermatogenesis.
Wrong - low LH and FSH point to suppression, not a chromosomal testicular failure.
Correct - stop androgens and recheck semen after months; recovery is usual.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man is assessed for 2 years of infertility. His testes are of normal size (20 mL each) but neither vas deferens can be felt in the scrotum. Semen analysis, repeated twice, shows a volume of 0.6 mL with no sperm. FSH, LH and testosterone are normal.
Which further test is most important for this couple?
o: CFTR gene mutation testing for both partners
Y-chromosome microdeletion testing for him only
Serum prolactin and pituitary MRI for him
Karyotype to look for Klinefelter syndrome
Antisperm antibody testing in both partners
mcq.e: Bilateral impalpable vasa with low-volume azoospermia and normal FSH indicate obstructive azoospermia from congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD). Most men with CBAVD carry CFTR mutations, so both partners need CFTR testing before sperm retrieval and ICSI to assess the risk of cystic fibrosis in the child. Normal FSH and testes make testicular failure (karyotype, Y microdeletion) unlikely.
w: Correct - CBAVD is linked to CFTR mutations; test both partners before ICSI.
Wrong - Y microdeletion testing is for non-obstructive azoospermia with high FSH.
Wrong - normal LH, FSH and testosterone exclude a pituitary cause.
Wrong - Klinefelter syndrome gives small firm testes and high FSH, not absent vasa.
Wrong - antisperm antibodies are irrelevant when there is no vas and no sperm.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 weeks of a dragging ache in the right side of his scrotum. On standing there is a soft swelling like a 'bag of worms' above the right testis; it does not empty when he lies flat. He has lost 3 kg, and urine dipstick shows blood 2+.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure; such swellings are common and benign
Advise scrotal support and review in 6 months
Refer for elective embolisation of the veins
Arrange urgent abdominal imaging for a mass
Start antibiotics for epididymo-orchitis
mcq.e: Most varicoceles are left-sided because the left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein. A new right-sided varicocele, or one that does not decompress on lying, suggests compression of the testicular vein or IVC by a renal or retroperitoneal mass - here supported by haematuria and weight loss. Urgent abdominal imaging comes before any treatment of the varicocele.
w: Wrong - a new right-sided, non-reducing varicocele is a red flag, not a benign finding.
Wrong - delay risks missing a renal cell carcinoma.
Wrong - treating the veins ignores the likely underlying mass.
Correct - exclude a renal or retroperitoneal mass with urgent abdominal imaging.
Wrong - there is no tender epididymis or fever; the swelling is venous.

mcq.stem:
A 41-year-old father of four had a vasectomy at a district hospital 4 weeks ago. He has had about 10 ejaculations since. He asks the Klinik Kesihatan doctor whether he and his wife can now stop using condoms.
What is the correct advice?
o: Stop contraception now, as the vas has been divided
Continue contraception until a semen test is clear
Continue contraception for one week after surgery
Stop contraception after his next 5 ejaculations
Continue contraception until his wife's next period
mcq.e: Vasectomy is not immediately effective because sperm remain stored in the vas beyond the cut. A post-vasectomy semen analysis is done at about 12 weeks (and after at least 20 ejaculations), and other contraception must continue until azoospermia is confirmed. Late recanalisation can rarely occur (about 1 in 2000).
w: Wrong - sperm persist beyond the cut for weeks after surgery.
Correct - continue contraception until post-vasectomy semen analysis (about 12 weeks) shows azoospermia.
Wrong - one week is far too short to clear stored sperm.
Wrong - the usual guide is at least 20 ejaculations plus a clear semen test, not 5.
Wrong - his wife's cycle has no bearing on sperm clearance.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old married man at a Klinik Kesihatan says the couple use latex condoms for family spacing, with baby oil as a lubricant. A condom burst last night, and his wife has been referred for emergency contraception.
What is the most important counselling point to prevent this happening again?
o: Use two condoms together for added protection
Switch to withdrawal as it is more reliable
Use water-based lubricant with latex condoms
Put the condom on just before ejaculation
Reuse condoms only after washing them well
mcq.e: Oil-based products such as baby oil, petroleum jelly and lotions weaken latex within minutes and cause breakage, so only water- or silicone-based lubricants should be used. Correct use also means a new condom from the start of every act. Double condoms increase friction and tearing, and withdrawal has a high typical-use failure rate (about 20%).
w: Wrong - two condoms rub together and are more likely to tear.
Wrong - withdrawal fails in about 1 in 5 couples a year with typical use.
Correct - oil-based lubricants degrade latex; use water-based lubricant.
Wrong - pre-ejaculate can carry sperm and STIs; wear it from the start.
Wrong - condoms are single-use only.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old man is assessed for primary infertility. He is 188 cm tall with sparse body hair and bilateral gynaecomastia. Both testes are small (4 mL) and firm. Two semen analyses show no sperm. FSH and LH are high and testosterone is low.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
Congenital absence of the vas deferens
Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism
Anabolic steroid-induced azoospermia
Bilateral varicocele
mcq.e: Small, firm testes with azoospermia, high gonadotrophins and low testosterone indicate primary testicular failure (non-obstructive azoospermia); with tall stature and gynaecomastia this is classic Klinefelter syndrome. Confirm with a karyotype and refer; some men still have sperm retrievable by micro-TESE for ICSI. Low LH and FSH would instead point to a pituitary cause or exogenous androgens.
w: Correct - primary testicular failure with tall stature and gynaecomastia; confirm by karyotype.
Wrong - CBAVD has normal testes, normal FSH and low semen volume.
Wrong - hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism has low, not high, LH and FSH.
Wrong - exogenous androgens suppress LH and FSH and raise testosterone.
Wrong - varicocele does not cause small firm testes, gynaecomastia and high FSH.

mcq.stem:
A 59-year-old man has nocturia once a night and a slightly weak stream. His IPSS is 6 and his quality-of-life score is 2 ('mostly satisfied'). Urinalysis, renal profile and fasting glucose are normal. DRE shows a smooth, mildly enlarged prostate; PSA is 1.1 ng/mL.
How should his symptoms be classified and managed?
o: Moderate symptoms; start tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily
Severe symptoms; refer to urology for TURP assessment
Moderate symptoms; start finasteride 5 mg daily
Severe symptoms; start combination drug therapy
Mild symptoms; watchful waiting and lifestyle advice
mcq.e: IPSS bands are mild 0-7, moderate 8-19 and severe 20-35. With mild, minimally bothersome symptoms and no red flags, watchful waiting with lifestyle advice (less fluid in the evening, less caffeine and alcohol, bladder training) and annual review is appropriate. Drug therapy is offered for bothersome moderate-severe symptoms.
w: Wrong - 6 is mild (moderate is 8-19), and he is not bothered enough to need a drug.
Wrong - severe is 20-35; surgery is not indicated.
Wrong - he is not moderate and has no large prostate needing a 5-ARI.
Wrong - combination therapy is for moderate-severe LUTS with a large prostate.
Correct - IPSS 0-7 = mild: watchful waiting, lifestyle advice and review.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man with known prostate enlargement attends a Klinik Kesihatan unable to pass urine for 8 hours. Three days ago a private clinic treated his cold with several medicines. His bladder is tender and palpable to the umbilicus.
Which of the medicines he was given is most likely to have precipitated this?
o: Paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly
Pseudoephedrine 60 mg TDS
Bromhexine 8 mg three times daily
Guaifenesin 200 mg 4-hourly
Vitamin C 500 mg daily
mcq.e: Sympathomimetic decongestants such as pseudoephedrine stimulate alpha receptors in the bladder neck and prostate, raising outlet resistance and precipitating acute retention in men with prostatic enlargement. Anticholinergics (including sedating antihistamines) and TCAs do so by weakening detrusor contraction. Always take a drug history in new or worsening LUTS.
w: Wrong - paracetamol has no effect on bladder outlet tone.
Correct - alpha-agonist decongestants raise bladder-neck tone and cause retention.
Wrong - bromhexine is a mucolytic without urinary effects.
Wrong - guaifenesin is an expectorant that does not affect voiding.
Wrong - vitamin C does not cause urinary retention.

mcq.stem:
A 71-year-old man complains of waking 4 times every night to pass urine; daytime voiding is normal. His 3-day bladder diary shows a 24-hour output of 2.4 L, of which 1.2 L is passed at night, with each void about 300 mL. He drinks 3 cups of tea after dinner. Fasting glucose is normal and IPSS voiding items score low.
What is the most likely cause of his nocturia?
o: Bladder outlet obstruction from an enlarged prostate
Detrusor overactivity reducing bladder capacity
Global polyuria from undiagnosed diabetes
Nocturnal polyuria with high night-time output
Chronic urinary retention with overflow
mcq.e: A bladder diary separates the causes of nocturia. Night-time output above one-third of the 24-hour total in an older man is nocturnal polyuria; normal void volumes (about 300 mL) argue against a small-capacity overactive bladder or obstruction, and 2.4 L a day is not global polyuria. Look for evening fluid and caffeine, diuretic timing, heart failure and obstructive sleep apnoea rather than starting prostate drugs.
w: Wrong - obstruction gives voiding symptoms and small frequent voids, not large night volumes.
Wrong - detrusor overactivity causes small urgent voids, not 300 mL voids.
Wrong - 2.4 L a day is not polyuria (above about 40 mL/kg), and glucose is normal.
Correct - half the output at night (above one-third) with normal void volumes is nocturnal polyuria.
Wrong - chronic retention gives a palpable bladder and overflow, not normal-volume voids.

mcq.stem:
A 49-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of difficulty starting his stream and a feeling of incomplete emptying. He has had severe low back pain with bilateral sciatica for a week after lifting heavy boxes. Examination shows numbness around the anus and reduced anal tone.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start tamsulosin and review in 2 weeks' time
Arrange outpatient ultrasound KUB and PSA
Emergency same-day referral for spinal MRI
Treat empirically for UTI with nitrofurantoin
Give a bladder diary to complete for 3 days
mcq.e: New voiding difficulty with back pain, bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia and reduced anal tone is cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise. It is a surgical emergency needing same-day MRI and decompression to save bladder, bowel and sexual function. This is why the neurological examination (lower limbs, anal tone, saddle sensation) is part of every LUTS assessment.
w: Wrong - an alpha-blocker treats prostatic obstruction and delays an emergency.
Wrong - outpatient tests are far too slow for cauda equina compression.
Correct - suspected cauda equina syndrome needs emergency MRI and surgical referral.
Wrong - there are no infective features; antibiotics miss the neurological cause.
Wrong - a bladder diary is for frequency or nocturia, not neurological red flags.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old man who has smoked for 40 years has 3 months of frequency, urgency and suprapubic discomfort. Urine dipstick shows blood 2+ on two occasions; urine cultures are sterile. The prostate is smooth and normal-sized on DRE.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Urgent urology referral for cystoscopy and imaging
Start an antimuscarinic for overactive bladder
Repeat urine culture and give empirical antibiotics
Start tamsulosin for presumed prostatic obstruction
Reassure and review the urine dipstick in 6 months
mcq.e: Storage (irritative) symptoms with persistent haematuria and sterile urine in an older smoker suggest bladder cancer (carcinoma in situ classically mimics cystitis), and smoking is its main risk factor. He needs urgent urology referral for cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging. Antibiotics or bladder drugs only delay the diagnosis.
w: Correct - haematuria with storage LUTS in a smoker needs cystoscopy to exclude a bladder tumour.
Wrong - antimuscarinics are used only after haematuria has been explained.
Wrong - cultures are already sterile; more antibiotics delay diagnosis.
Wrong - the prostate is normal and his symptoms are storage, not voiding.
Wrong - haematuria is a red flag and must not be watched for months.

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old man's wife reports that he has recently started wetting the bed at night. He has had a poor stream for years but no pain. After he voids, there is a non-tender, dull swelling arising from the pelvis to above the umbilicus. Creatinine is 210 micromol/L (previously 95).
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Overactive bladder with urge incontinence
Stress urinary incontinence from weak sphincter
Acute urinary retention from a blood clot
Nocturnal polyuria from heart failure
Chronic retention with overflow incontinence
mcq.e: A painless, palpable bladder after voiding with new nocturnal incontinence and rising creatinine is high-pressure chronic retention with overflow - a LUTS red flag. He needs catheterisation (watching for post-obstructive diuresis) and urology referral. Acute retention is painful, and overactive bladder does not leave a large residual.
w: Wrong - overactive bladder does not cause a palpable residual bladder or renal impairment.
Wrong - stress incontinence occurs with coughing or straining, not at night with a full bladder.
Wrong - acute retention is sudden and painful, not painless after years of symptoms.
Wrong - nocturnal polyuria causes frequent voids, not a distended bladder.
Correct - painless distended bladder, nocturnal overflow and rising creatinine = chronic retention.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old man has a bothersome weak stream, hesitancy and nocturia twice nightly. IPSS is 15 with a quality-of-life score of 4. Urinalysis and creatinine are normal. Ultrasound shows a prostate volume of 25 mL with a small residual; PSA is 1.0 ng/mL.
Which is the most appropriate first-line drug?
o: Finasteride 5 mg once daily
Tamsulosin 400 micrograms once daily
Oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily
Dutasteride 0.5 mg once daily
Desmopressin 100 micrograms at night
mcq.e: Bothersome moderate LUTS (IPSS 8-19) without complications is treated first with an alpha-1 blocker, which relaxes prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle and works within days to weeks. 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors are reserved for enlarged prostates (over 30-40 mL or PSA over 1.5 ng/mL) and take months to act. His symptoms are voiding-predominant, so an antimuscarinic is not the first choice.
w: Wrong - finasteride needs a larger prostate (over 30-40 mL) and takes 3-6 months to work.
Correct - an alpha-blocker is first-line for bothersome moderate LUTS with a small prostate.
Wrong - an antimuscarinic targets storage symptoms; his are mainly voiding.
Wrong - dutasteride, like finasteride, suits enlarged prostates only.
Wrong - desmopressin treats nocturnal polyuria and risks hyponatraemia in older men.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old man has taken tamsulosin for 3 months with only partial relief. IPSS is 22. Ultrasound shows a prostate volume of 60 mL and a post-void residual of 60 mL; PSA is 3.8 ng/mL and DRE shows a smooth, symmetrical gland. Creatinine is normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Stop tamsulosin and switch to an antimuscarinic
Double the tamsulosin dose to 800 micrograms
Add finasteride while continuing the tamsulosin
Add oxybutynin to the current tamsulosin dose
Stop tamsulosin and start desmopressin at night
mcq.e: Moderate-to-severe LUTS with a large prostate (over 30-40 mL) or PSA over 1.5 ng/mL carries a high risk of progression; combining an alpha-blocker with a 5-ARI beats either alone for symptoms and for reducing retention and surgery. The 5-ARI takes 3-6 months to work, so the alpha-blocker is continued. Finasteride will halve his PSA, so record this baseline.
w: Wrong - his symptoms are voiding-predominant and he still needs the alpha-blocker.
Wrong - a higher dose adds side effects without treating gland size.
Correct - large prostate + moderate-severe LUTS: combination alpha-blocker and 5-ARI.
Wrong - antimuscarinics are not the add-on for voiding symptoms in a large gland.
Wrong - desmopressin treats nocturnal polyuria, not prostatic enlargement.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old man has taken tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily for 2 years with good control of his urinary symptoms. He is due for cataract surgery next month and asks whether anything needs to be done about his tablets.
What is the most important advice?
o: Stop tamsulosin the day before surgery
Switch tamsulosin to doxazosin before surgery
Double the dose to prevent retention post-op
Inform the eye surgeon that he takes tamsulosin
Add finasteride to cover the perioperative period
mcq.e: Tamsulosin (and to a lesser degree other alpha-blockers) causes intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, with iris billowing and poor pupil dilation during cataract surgery. The risk persists even after the drug is stopped, so the key step is telling the ophthalmologist, who can plan iris hooks or intracameral drugs. Stopping the drug is unnecessary and may precipitate retention.
w: Wrong - floppy iris syndrome can occur even months after stopping the drug.
Wrong - doxazosin also carries the risk and offers no advantage.
Wrong - dose escalation increases side effects and does not help.
Correct - the surgeon must know so they can prepare for floppy iris syndrome.
Wrong - finasteride does not replace the alpha-blocker or affect the iris risk.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man has taken finasteride 5 mg daily for 2 years for prostate enlargement. His PSA before starting was 2.2 ng/mL. A repeat PSA today is 2.4 ng/mL. DRE shows a smooth gland and he is well.
How should this PSA result be interpreted?
o: Suspicious, as PSA should have halved on finasteride
Normal, as a PSA under 4 ng/mL excludes cancer
Reassuring, as the PSA has barely changed in 2 years
Uninterpretable, so stop checking PSA on finasteride
Due to BPH only, so increase the finasteride dose
mcq.e: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors lower PSA by about 50% after 6-12 months, so the measured value should be doubled (here about 4.8 ng/mL). A PSA that fails to fall, or rises, on a 5-ARI is suspicious for prostate cancer and needs evaluation and urology referral. Nominal values under 4 ng/mL do not reassure in this setting.
w: Correct - PSA should halve on finasteride; a stable or rising value is suspicious.
Wrong - no PSA cut-off excludes cancer, and this value must be doubled.
Wrong - the expected fall did not occur, which is the warning sign.
Wrong - PSA remains useful if interpreted correctly (double it).
Wrong - treated BPH should not hold PSA up, and finasteride has a fixed 5 mg dose.

mcq.stem:
A 75-year-old man with known prostate enlargement presents to a Klinik Kesihatan in agony, unable to pass urine for 10 hours after a heavy drinking session. His bladder is tense and tender to the umbilicus. Vital signs are stable.
What is the most appropriate immediate step?
o: Give oral tamsulosin and wait 2 hours for voiding
Prescribe IV fluids to stimulate urine production
Give oral analgesia and arrange urology clinic next week
Arrange urgent ultrasound KUB before any intervention
Insert a urethral catheter and record drained volume
mcq.e: Painful acute urinary retention needs immediate bladder drainage by urethral catheterisation, recording the residual volume (which helps grade severity and predicts outcome). Precipitants (alcohol, drugs, constipation, UTI) are addressed, an alpha-blocker is started and he is referred for a trial without catheter. Waiting or imaging first only prolongs pain and risks bladder damage.
w: Wrong - an alpha-blocker helps a later trial without catheter but does not relieve retention now.
Wrong - fluids increase bladder distension and pain.
Wrong - he needs drainage today, not next week.
Wrong - imaging is not needed before relieving clinically obvious retention.
Correct - catheterise now and record the drained volume, then refer for TWOC.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old man has been on tamsulosin and finasteride for 3 years. At review his creatinine has risen from 95 to 180 micromol/L over 6 months. Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis and a post-void residual of 450 mL. He feels his stream is 'about the same'.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue drugs and repeat renal profile in 3 months
Refer to urology for obstructive uropathy and surgery
Add an antimuscarinic to relax the overactive bladder
Stop the finasteride, which is damaging his kidneys
Start furosemide to improve urine flow and clearance
mcq.e: Renal impairment and bilateral hydronephrosis with a large residual indicate obstructive uropathy from chronic retention - an indication for urology referral (catheter drainage, then usually TURP) however little he is bothered. Rising creatinine, hydronephrosis, recurrent retention, recurrent UTI, haematuria and bladder stones move BPH from medical to surgical care.
w: Wrong - waiting 3 months risks irreversible renal damage.
Correct - obstructive uropathy is an indication for urology referral and surgery.
Wrong - antimuscarinics worsen retention with a large residual.
Wrong - finasteride does not harm the kidneys; the obstruction does.
Wrong - diuretics increase bladder filling and do not relieve obstruction.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old man has frequency, urgency, nocturia, a weak stream and straining. Ultrasound shows a prostate volume of 45 mL and a post-void residual of 280 mL. Creatinine is normal. He asks for a tablet to 'stop the rushing'.
Which drug is most likely to precipitate acute urinary retention and should be avoided?
o: Tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily
Finasteride 5 mg daily
Solifenacin 5 mg daily
Tadalafil 5 mg daily
Doxazosin 4 mg at night
mcq.e: Antimuscarinics such as solifenacin and oxybutynin reduce detrusor contraction; in a man with a large post-void residual (over about 200 mL) they can precipitate acute retention. Check the residual before adding any storage drug. Alpha-blockers, 5-ARIs and tadalafil improve outflow or are neutral.
w: Wrong - tamsulosin improves outflow and is appropriate here.
Wrong - finasteride shrinks the prostate and reduces retention risk.
Correct - an antimuscarinic with a residual of 280 mL risks acute retention.
Wrong - tadalafil 5 mg daily is used for BPH-LUTS and does not cause retention.
Wrong - doxazosin relaxes the bladder neck and helps voiding.

mcq.stem:
A 69-year-old man with bothersome voiding LUTS was started on terazosin 2 mg, which he took with breakfast. An hour after the first tablet he fainted while standing at the market and recovered quickly. ECG and glucose are normal; BP is 132/80 mmHg lying with no postural drop now.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop all BPH drugs permanently and refer for TURP
Switch to finasteride, which works just as quickly
Continue the same dose but take it with breakfast
Restart at 1 mg at bedtime and titrate up gradually
Add fludrocortisone to prevent further postural drops
mcq.e: Non-uroselective alpha-blockers (terazosin, doxazosin) cause first-dose postural hypotension and syncope. They are started at a low dose (terazosin 1 mg) at bedtime and titrated, or a uroselective agent such as tamsulosin is used. Note: the slide gives terazosin 2-8 mg ON; the usual practice is to start at 1 mg at night and titrate to 2-10 mg.
w: Wrong - a first-dose effect is not a reason to abandon medical therapy.
Wrong - finasteride takes 3-6 months to act and needs a large prostate.
Wrong - a morning dose while active is what caused the syncope.
Correct - low dose at bedtime with slow titration avoids first-dose hypotension.
Wrong - adding a mineralocorticoid is inappropriate for an avoidable drug effect.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old man has moderate bothersome LUTS (IPSS 12) and also reports erectile difficulty for a year. Prostate volume is 28 mL and PSA is 0.9 ng/mL. He has no cardiac disease and takes no nitrates. He would like a single daily tablet if possible.
Which drug best treats both problems?
o: Tadalafil 5 mg once daily
Sildenafil 50 mg on demand
Finasteride 5 mg once daily
Dutasteride 0.5 mg once daily
Terazosin 2 mg at night
mcq.e: Daily low-dose tadalafil (5 mg) improves both LUTS from BPH and erectile function by relaxing smooth muscle in the prostate, bladder neck and corpora. On-demand sildenafil treats ED only. 5-ARIs need a larger gland and commonly worsen erectile function and libido, and the nitrate contraindication applies to tadalafil as to all PDE5 inhibitors.
w: Correct - daily tadalafil 5 mg treats BPH-LUTS and ED together.
Wrong - on-demand sildenafil is not used for LUTS.
Wrong - finasteride suits large glands and can worsen ED and libido.
Wrong - dutasteride shares these sexual side effects and needs a large prostate.
Wrong - terazosin helps LUTS but does nothing for erectile function.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of fever (39.2 C), rigors, dysuria, frequency and severe pain between the scrotum and anus. There is no loin tenderness and the scrotum and testes are normal. A gentle DRE finds an exquisitely tender, warm, swollen prostate. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Acute pyelonephritis
Acute epididymo-orchitis
Chronic pelvic pain syndrome
Acute cystitis (lower UTI)
Acute bacterial prostatitis
mcq.e: Fever, rigors, perineal pain and dysuria with a tender, warm, swollen prostate is acute bacterial prostatitis, most often due to E. coli. Simple cystitis does not cause high fever or a tender prostate, and pyelonephritis gives loin pain and renal-angle tenderness. CP/CPPS is chronic (at least 3 months) and afebrile.
w: Wrong - there is no loin pain or renal-angle tenderness.
Wrong - the scrotum and testes are normal.
Wrong - CP/CPPS is chronic, afebrile and has no positive urine.
Wrong - cystitis does not cause high fever, rigors or a tender prostate.
Correct - systemic features plus a tender, warm, swollen prostate = acute bacterial prostatitis.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man has acute bacterial prostatitis diagnosed at a Klinik Kesihatan. He is febrile (38.3 C) but haemodynamically stable, passing urine well and tolerating oral fluids. He has no drug allergies. Urine culture has been sent.
Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
o: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for 5 days
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 3 days
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 14 days
Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 7 days
Cefuroxime 250 mg BD for 5 days
mcq.e: Mild acute bacterial prostatitis is treated with an agent that penetrates the prostate well - ciprofloxacin 500-750 mg BD (or co-trimoxazole) - for a prolonged course of 14 days, with many guidelines advising 2-4 weeks. Short courses suited to cystitis lead to relapse and chronic bacterial prostatitis. Nitrofurantoin does not reach therapeutic levels in prostatic tissue.
w: Wrong - nitrofurantoin does not penetrate the prostate and the course is too short.
Wrong - a 3-day cystitis course leads to relapse and chronic prostatitis.
Correct - a prostate-penetrating fluoroquinolone for a prolonged 14-day course.
Wrong - amoxicillin penetrates prostate poorly and 7 days is too short.
Wrong - a 5-day course is too short for prostatic infection.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man with fever, perineal pain and dysuria is found on gentle DRE to have a hot, very tender prostate. The house officer wants to confirm the diagnosis and isolate the organism before starting antibiotics.
Which procedure should be avoided?
o: Gentle digital rectal examination
Prostatic massage to obtain secretions
Midstream urine for Gram stain and culture
Blood cultures if he appears septic
Serum CRP and full blood count
mcq.e: In acute bacterial prostatitis, vigorous prostatic massage is extremely painful and can push bacteria into the bloodstream, causing bacteraemia and sepsis. The organism is identified from a midstream urine culture (and blood cultures if septic). Expressed prostatic secretions after massage are used only in suspected chronic bacterial prostatitis.
w: Wrong - a gentle DRE is part of the assessment.
Correct - massage of an acutely infected prostate risks bacteraemia and sepsis.
Wrong - midstream urine culture is the key test to isolate the organism.
Wrong - blood cultures are appropriate if he is septic.
Wrong - CRP and FBC help assess severity and are safe.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has 3 days of perineal pain, dysuria and rigors. Temperature is 39.5 C, BP 92/58 mmHg and pulse 118/min. He has vomited twice and cannot keep fluids down. The prostate is very tender on gentle DRE.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral ciprofloxacin and review at the clinic in 48 hours
Oral co-trimoxazole for 14 days with paracetamol
Prostatic massage to drain pus, then oral antibiotics
Admit for IV amoxicillin plus gentamicin and fluids
IM ceftriaxone once, then oral antibiotics at home
mcq.e: Hypotension, tachycardia, vomiting and diabetes make this severe acute bacterial prostatitis with sepsis. He needs admission for IV fluids and IV antibiotics (amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 4-6 mg/kg/day, as on the slide), stepping down to oral therapy to complete 2-4 weeks. If retention develops, suprapubic catheterisation is preferred.
w: Wrong - a septic, vomiting patient cannot be managed with oral therapy at home.
Wrong - oral treatment is for mild infection in a stable patient.
Wrong - massage of an acutely infected prostate risks worsening sepsis.
Correct - sepsis and vomiting need admission for IV amoxicillin + gentamicin and fluids.
Wrong - a single IM dose is inadequate for a septic, hypotensive patient.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man has had three urinary infections with the same E. coli in 8 months, despite 5-day antibiotic courses. Between episodes he is afebrile but has perineal discomfort and pain after ejaculation. DRE shows a mildly tender prostate. Urine after prostatic massage has more white cells and bacteria than urine before massage.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 4-6 weeks
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for 7 days
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 3 days
Tamsulosin alone, with no antibiotic at all
Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 2 weeks
mcq.e: Recurrent UTI with the same organism, symptoms for over 3 months and a positive post-massage specimen indicate chronic bacterial prostatitis, often after undertreated acute infection. It needs a prolonged course of a prostate-penetrating antibiotic - ciprofloxacin 500-750 mg BD for 4-6 weeks - with NSAIDs for pain and an alpha-blocker if voiding symptoms. Short courses are why his infections keep returning.
w: Correct - chronic bacterial prostatitis needs 4-6 weeks of a fluoroquinolone.
Wrong - nitrofurantoin does not penetrate the prostate.
Wrong - short courses are the reason for his relapses.
Wrong - an alpha-blocker is an adjunct; the infection still needs antibiotics.
Wrong - amoxicillin penetrates the prostate poorly.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old man has had 5 months of perineal and penile-tip pain with discomfort after ejaculation. He is afebrile. Repeated urine cultures and STI tests are negative, and one 6-week course of ciprofloxacin gave no benefit. DRE shows a mildly tender prostate. He reports heavy work stress and poor sleep.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: A further 6-week course of a different antibiotic
Repeated prostatic massage to drain the prostate
Refer for transurethral resection of the prostate
Long-term low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis
Multimodal care with pelvic floor physiotherapy
mcq.e: Pelvic pain for at least 3 of the previous 6 months with no evidence of infection is chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome, the commonest form of prostatitis and a diagnosis of exclusion. Management is multimodal: alpha-blocker for voiding symptoms, analgesics, pelvic floor physiotherapy, stress management and psychological support. Antibiotics are tried only once, early; repeating them after failure is not helpful.
w: Wrong - antibiotics are only worth one early trial; repeat courses do not help.
Wrong - repeated massage has no proven benefit and may aggravate pain.
Wrong - surgery has no role in CP/CPPS.
Wrong - there is no infection to prevent.
Correct - CP/CPPS needs multimodal care, including physiotherapy and stress management.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old man with diabetes has been taking oral ciprofloxacin for 4 days for acute bacterial prostatitis. He remains febrile at 38.9 C with worsening perineal pain. Gentle DRE now reveals a fluctuant area in the right lobe of the prostate.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Switch to oral amoxicillin and review in a week
Add an NSAID; fever often persists for 2 weeks
Urgent imaging and referral for suspected abscess
Stop antibiotics and send urine for repeat culture
Perform prostatic massage to drain the infection
mcq.e: Failure to improve within 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics, especially in a diabetic, with a fluctuant prostate suggests a prostatic abscess. He needs urgent referral for transrectal ultrasound or CT and drainage, with IV antibiotics. Massage could cause bacteraemia, and switching to a poorly penetrating oral drug delays treatment.
w: Wrong - amoxicillin penetrates poorly and a week's delay is unsafe.
Wrong - persistent fever beyond 72 hours is not expected and needs investigation.
Correct - non-response with a fluctuant prostate suggests abscess: image and refer.
Wrong - stopping antibiotics in active infection is dangerous.
Wrong - massaging an infected prostate risks sepsis.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old lorry driver is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan by his wife. Over 3 months he has become irritable with angry outbursts, is drinking more, works extra shifts and sleeps poorly. He complains of back pain and tiredness but denies feeling sad.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Advise anger management and alcohol reduction only
Screen for depression with the PHQ-9 and assess risk
Prescribe zolpidem for insomnia and review in a month
Refer to physiotherapy for his chronic back pain
Reassure; irritability is common with job stress
mcq.e: Depression in men often presents differently: irritability, anger, alcohol use, overworking and somatic complaints rather than sadness, so it is easily missed. Active screening (PHQ-2/PHQ-9 or DASS-21) with an assessment of suicide risk is needed. Treating each symptom separately misses the unifying diagnosis.
w: Wrong - this treats the behaviour but misses possible depression.
Correct - 'male-pattern' depression needs active screening and risk assessment.
Wrong - a hypnotic treats one symptom and may worsen risk with alcohol.
Wrong - his back pain may be a somatic feature of depression.
Wrong - reassurance misses a treatable, potentially dangerous condition.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man was retrenched 2 months ago and his wife has moved out. He drinks heavily most nights. At a Klinik Kesihatan he scores positive on PHQ-9 item 9. On direct questioning he says he plans to hang himself this weekend and has bought a rope.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start fluoxetine 20 mg and review in two weeks
Give the Talian HEAL number and arrange follow-up
Book a routine appointment at the psychiatric clinic
Keep him supervised and arrange same-day psychiatry
Ask his wife to take him home and remove the rope
mcq.e: Male sex, recent losses, heavy alcohol use and a specific plan with means make his suicide risk high. He must not be left alone and needs same-day psychiatric assessment (or the emergency department), with removal of means and family involvement as part of safety planning. Antidepressants, helplines and routine appointments are not adequate for imminent risk.
w: Wrong - antidepressants take weeks to act and do not address imminent risk.
Wrong - a helpline is an adjunct, not enough for a man with a plan and means.
Wrong - a routine appointment is far too slow for high immediate risk.
Correct - a plan with means = high risk: supervision and same-day psychiatric assessment.
Wrong - sending him home without assessment leaves him at serious risk.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man started sertraline 50 mg for moderate depression 6 weeks ago. His wife says his mood had improved, but he has quietly stopped the tablets. When asked privately, he admits he could not ejaculate and felt embarrassed to mention it.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Discuss it openly and switch him to mirtazapine
Advise him to stop antidepressants altogether
Add sildenafil and double the sertraline dose
Switch to paroxetine, which spares sexual function
Reassure him it is unrelated to the medication
mcq.e: SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction (delayed ejaculation, low libido, ED) is common and a frequent hidden reason why men default. Ask about it routinely and manage it - for example by switching to an antidepressant with fewer sexual effects such as mirtazapine. Paroxetine has the highest rate of sexual dysfunction among SSRIs.
w: Correct - address the side effect openly and switch to a sexually sparing antidepressant.
Wrong - stopping after 6 weeks risks relapse; he needs at least 6-12 months of treatment.
Wrong - doubling the SSRI dose worsens the ejaculatory problem.
Wrong - paroxetine causes the most sexual dysfunction of the SSRIs.
Wrong - delayed ejaculation is a well-recognised SSRI effect.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man started fluoxetine 20 mg for depression 10 days ago at a Klinik Kesihatan. He returns saying 'it is not working' and he wants to stop because he sees no change. He has mild nausea but no suicidal thoughts.
What is the most appropriate response?
o: Stop fluoxetine, as no response by 10 days means failure
Double the dose now to speed up the response
Switch to a different SSRI starting tomorrow
Add diazepam and stop fluoxetine next week
Explain onset takes 2-4 weeks and review soon
mcq.e: Men often doubt a treatment that does not work quickly and are at high risk of defaulting. Antidepressants take about 2-4 weeks to start working, and response is judged at 4-6 weeks; early nausea usually settles. Clear explanation, early follow-up and agreed goals improve adherence.
w: Wrong - 10 days is too early to judge response.
Wrong - raising the dose early increases side effects without faster benefit.
Wrong - switching before an adequate trial is premature.
Wrong - benzodiazepines are not a treatment for depression and risk dependence.
Correct - explain the delayed onset and arrange early review to prevent default.

mcq.stem:
A family medicine specialist at a Klinik Kesihatan is planning outreach for men with psychological distress in her district. She wants to target the men least likely to seek treatment on their own.
Based on factors affecting men's help-seeking, which man is least likely to seek treatment?
o: A 60-year-old retired teacher with a degree
A 55-year-old engineer with a master's degree
A 22-year-old labourer who left school at 15
A 50-year-old lecturer with a doctorate
A 65-year-old pensioner with a diploma
mcq.e: Older age and a higher education level significantly increase the likelihood that men seek treatment. Young men with little formal education are therefore the hardest to reach. Outreach should go to them - workplaces, community and social media - rather than wait for them to attend.
w: Wrong - older age and tertiary education both favour help-seeking.
Wrong - higher education increases help-seeking.
Correct - young age and low education both reduce help-seeking.
Wrong - a doctorate-level education favours help-seeking.
Wrong - older age increases the likelihood of seeking treatment.

mcq.stem:
A Klinik Kesihatan in a rural mukim finds that local Malay Muslim men rarely attend for mental health problems. Most work in plantations and see the clinic as a place for women and children. The team wants a strategy to reduce stigma among these men.
Which strategy is most likely to reach them?
o: Posters in the antenatal room of the clinic
Messages in the Friday khutbah at the mosque
A weekday 9 am clinic for mental health only
Leaflets mailed to women in the household
An online forum for clinicians about stigma
mcq.e: Men are more receptive to messages from voices they already trust. The seminar recommends involving religious leaders - for example through the Khutbah Jumaat or ceramah maghrib - alongside national campaigns with the message 'it's okay not to be okay'. Clinic-based posters and weekday clinics miss men who do not attend.
w: Wrong - men who do not attend the clinic will not see antenatal-room posters.
Correct - religious leaders reach men directly through trusted Friday sermons.
Wrong - weekday daytime clinics clash with work and keep men away.
Wrong - this bypasses the men themselves.
Wrong - clinician forums do not reach the target community.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 months of low mood, poor sleep, loss of interest and poor concentration at work. His PHQ-9 score is 12; item 9 (self-harm) scores 0. He has no psychotic features and no past psychiatric history.
How is his depression graded and managed?
o: Mild; watchful waiting and review in two weeks
Severe; urgent referral for inpatient psychiatry
Minimal; reassure and discharge from follow-up
Moderate; antidepressant plus psychological therapy
Moderately severe; start two antidepressants
mcq.e: PHQ-9 bands: 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-19 moderately severe and 20-27 severe. A score of 12 is moderate depression, managed in primary care with an antidepressant (e.g. an SSRI) together with psychological intervention and early follow-up. Item 9 must always be checked; a positive answer needs same-day risk assessment.
w: Wrong - mild is 5-9; 12 is moderate.
Wrong - severe is 20-27, and he has no risk features needing admission.
Wrong - minimal is under 5.
Correct - PHQ-9 10-14 is moderate: antidepressant with psychological therapy.
Wrong - 12 is not moderately severe, and two antidepressants are never first-line.

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 months of tiredness. He has no abdominal pain, no change in bowel habit and no visible rectal bleeding. Hb is 9.2 g/dL, MCV 68 fL and ferritin 6 microg/L. He eats a normal mixed diet. Abdominal examination and DRE are normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer for both colonoscopy and upper GI endoscopy
Start oral iron and recheck the Hb in three months
Arrange iFOBT and refer only if it is positive
Check thalassaemia screen before any referral
Advise a high-iron diet and review in 6 weeks
mcq.e: Men have no physiological blood loss, so iron deficiency anaemia in a man is occult gastrointestinal bleeding - classically right-sided colon cancer - until proven otherwise. He needs referral for colonoscopy and OGDS. iFOBT is a screening test for asymptomatic people, and iron alone masks the cause.
w: Correct - unexplained IDA in a man needs lower and upper GI endoscopy.
Wrong - iron without investigation can mask a caecal cancer.
Wrong - iFOBT is for asymptomatic screening; a negative result must not reassure.
Wrong - low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, not thalassaemia trait.
Wrong - diet does not explain IDA in a man eating normally.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 months of looser, more frequent stools and dark red blood mixed in the stool. He has lost 4 kg unintentionally. Abdominal examination and DRE are normal; Hb is 12.1 g/dL.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Arrange iFOBT and refer if the result is positive
Treat as haemorrhoids and review in 6 weeks
Refer urgently for colonoscopy without iFOBT
Request serum CEA and refer only if it is raised
Give a high-fibre diet trial for one month
mcq.e: Rectal bleeding with a change in bowel habit and weight loss are red flags for colorectal cancer, and symptomatic patients go straight to urgent colonoscopy. iFOBT is a screening test for asymptomatic, average-risk adults; a negative result could falsely reassure. CEA is for baseline and surveillance, not diagnosis.
w: Wrong - iFOBT is not for symptomatic patients and may falsely reassure.
Wrong - blood mixed with stool plus weight loss is not explained by haemorrhoids.
Correct - red-flag symptoms need direct urgent referral for colonoscopy.
Wrong - CEA is neither sensitive nor specific enough for diagnosis.
Wrong - a dietary trial delays the diagnosis of a possible cancer.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man with no bowel symptoms attends a Klinik Kesihatan health screen. He has no family history of bowel cancer or polyps and no inflammatory bowel disease. Hb is normal. He asks whether he should be screened for bowel cancer.
What is the recommended screening approach in Malaysia?
o: Colonoscopy every year from now
Serum CEA as an annual blood test
CT colonography every two years
Guaiac FOBT after a meat-free diet
iFOBT as the first screening test
mcq.e: Malaysia's national programme screens asymptomatic, average-risk adults aged 50-75 with the immunochemical faecal occult blood test (iFOBT) at the Klinik Kesihatan. It detects human haemoglobin, so no dietary restriction is needed; a positive test leads to colonoscopy. CEA is not a screening test.
w: Wrong - yearly colonoscopy is excessive for an average-risk man.
Wrong - CEA is for surveillance after treatment, not screening.
Wrong - CT colonography is not the national screening test.
Wrong - the programme uses immunochemical FOBT, which needs no diet restriction.
Correct - iFOBT is the screening test for average-risk adults aged 50-75.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man with no symptoms attends a Klinik Kesihatan. His father was diagnosed with colorectal cancer at the age of 46. There are no other affected relatives and no known hereditary syndrome. Examination is normal.
What is the most appropriate screening plan?
o: iFOBT yearly starting at age 50
Colonoscopy now, as he is past age 36
Colonoscopy starting at age 50
iFOBT now, and colonoscopy only if positive
No screening until he has symptoms
mcq.e: A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer puts him at increased risk, so he is screened by colonoscopy rather than iFOBT. Screening starts at age 40 or 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis, whichever is earlier - here 46 minus 10 = 36. He is already 38, so colonoscopy should be arranged now.
w: Wrong - average-risk iFOBT from 50 is too late and too insensitive for him.
Correct - colonoscopy from 10 years before the relative's diagnosis (36) - so now.
Wrong - starting at 50 ignores his family history.
Wrong - increased-risk men are screened by colonoscopy, not iFOBT.
Wrong - waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose of screening.

mcq.stem:
A 56-year-old man had an iFOBT at a Klinik Kesihatan health screen, which is positive. He has no bowel symptoms. He says he has had haemorrhoids for years and occasionally sees bright red blood on the toilet paper. Abdominal examination is normal and proctoscopy shows grade 1 internal haemorrhoids. Hb is 14.1 g/dL.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Repeat the iFOBT in 3 months after treating the piles
Treat the haemorrhoids and resume yearly iFOBT
Refer for colonoscopy to evaluate the positive result
Request serum CEA and refer only if it is raised
Arrange a barium enema to look for a colonic mass
mcq.e: A positive iFOBT must be followed by **colonoscopy**, whatever other source of bleeding is found. Haemorrhoids are common and can coexist with an adenoma or cancer, so blaming the result on piles is the classic trap. Repeating the test or checking CEA only delays the diagnosis.
w: Wrong - a negative repeat does not cancel a positive screen; it only delays colonoscopy.
Wrong - haemorrhoids do not explain away a positive iFOBT; a neoplasm may coexist.
Correct - every positive iFOBT needs colonoscopy, the diagnostic test.
Wrong - CEA is insensitive for early cancer and is not a diagnostic or triage test.
Wrong - barium enema is inferior and cannot take a biopsy; colonoscopy is the standard.

mcq.stem:
A 54-year-old man with no symptoms asks at a Klinik Kesihatan for a 'cancer blood test' because a colleague was recently diagnosed with bowel cancer. He has no family history, no bowel symptoms, a normal examination and Hb 14.6 g/dL. He has never had colorectal screening.
What is the best response?
o: Offer iFOBT; CEA is for baseline and surveillance
Request CEA, as a normal level excludes colorectal cancer
Request CEA and arrange colonoscopy only if it is raised
Offer a CEA test yearly, alternating with yearly iFOBT
Refer for CT of the abdomen and pelvis as a screen
mcq.e: CEA is neither sensitive nor specific enough to screen for or diagnose colorectal cancer; the slides place it at **baseline** (after diagnosis) and in **surveillance** for recurrence. An average-risk man aged 50-75 should be offered **iFOBT**, with colonoscopy if positive. A normal CEA gives false reassurance.
w: Correct - iFOBT is the national screening test; CEA is a baseline and surveillance marker.
Wrong - CEA is normal in many early cancers, so it cannot exclude CRC.
Wrong - using CEA as a gatekeeper would miss most early cancers.
Wrong - CEA has no role in screening, alternating or not.
Wrong - CT is a staging test, not a screening test for average-risk men.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old man was referred from a Klinik Kesihatan with rectal bleeding and tenesmus. Colonoscopy and biopsy confirm adenocarcinoma 8 cm from the anal verge. Before deciding on neoadjuvant therapy, the surgical team wants to define the depth of invasion, nodal involvement and the circumferential resection margin.
Which investigation best answers this question?
o: CT of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis
Whole-body FDG PET-CT scan
Serial serum CEA levels
Repeat colonoscopy and biopsy
High-resolution MRI of the pelvis
mcq.e: **MRI pelvis** is the key local staging test for rectal cancer: it shows T stage, nodes and a threatened circumferential margin, which decide neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy. CT thorax, abdomen and pelvis is for distant staging (liver, lungs). FDG PET-CT is reserved for suspected recurrence, not routine initial staging.
w: Wrong - CT TAP is for distant staging and gives poor detail of the mesorectal margin.
Wrong - PET-CT is for suspected recurrence and is not routine for initial staging.
Wrong - CEA is a baseline and surveillance marker, not an anatomical staging test.
Wrong - the diagnosis is already confirmed; repeat endoscopy adds no staging data.
Correct - MRI pelvis stages the rectal tumour locally and maps the circumferential margin.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old man, a current smoker of 40 pack-years, attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 5 weeks of cough and two episodes of blood-streaked sputum. He has lost 4 kg. Examination is unremarkable and SpO2 is 97% on air. Two sputum AFB smears last week were negative and a chest X-ray today is reported as normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure him, as a normal chest X-ray excludes cancer
Refer urgently to a lung specialist for further assessment
Give a course of amoxicillin and review him in 6 weeks
Repeat the chest X-ray in 3 months if symptoms persist
Start an inhaled steroid for a presumed COPD flare
mcq.e: The slide pathway: if the chest X-ray is abnormal **or** clinical suspicion remains high despite a normal film, refer **urgently** to a lung specialist for CT and further assessment. A chest X-ray can miss small, central or hilar tumours, and haemoptysis with weight loss in a heavy smoker is high suspicion. Antibiotic trials or watchful waiting only delay diagnosis in a cancer where 95% of Malaysian cases already present at stage III-IV.
w: Wrong - a normal CXR does not exclude lung cancer, especially central tumours.
Correct - high clinical suspicion warrants urgent referral even with a normal CXR.
Wrong - there are no signs of infection; an antibiotic trial delays diagnosis.
Wrong - a 3-month wait is unsafe with haemoptysis and weight loss.
Wrong - there is no evidence of COPD, and steroids would only delay diagnosis.

mcq.stem:
A Klinik Kesihatan is drawing up a list of men to refer for lung cancer screening, using the criteria on the seminar slides. Five men, none with respiratory symptoms, are being considered.
Which man is eligible for low-dose CT screening?
o: A 41-year-old who has smoked daily for 22 years
A 52-year-old who smoked for 8 years and then stopped
A 79-year-old ex-smoker who smoked for 45 years
A 58-year-old ex-smoker who smoked for 30 years
A 36-year-old never-smoker whose father had lung cancer
mcq.e: The slides recommend **LDCT** for people aged **45-75** with **at least 20 years** of smoking, current or former, and for high-risk never-smokers **over 40** with a significant family history. The 58-year-old ex-smoker meets both the age and smoking criteria; former smokers remain at raised risk for many years. Each of the others fails on age or smoking duration.
w: Wrong - 22 years of smoking qualifies, but he is under 45.
Wrong - he is in the age band but has only 8 years of smoking.
Wrong - he is above the upper age limit of 75.
Correct - aged 45-75 with at least 20 years of smoking, current or former.
Wrong - family history qualifies a never-smoker only once he is over 40.

mcq.stem:
A 67-year-old former smoker (30 years, stopped 5 years ago) attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 4 weeks of persistent cough, poor appetite and his second chest infection in two months. He is afebrile, SpO2 is 96% and there are no focal chest signs. He has read about lung cancer screening and asks to join the programme.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Book him into the routine LDCT screening programme
Prescribe a cough linctus and review in 3 months
Send sputum for cytology before any imaging
Arrange a chest X-ray and assess clinical suspicion
Refer for spirometry to confirm COPD first
mcq.e: Screening is for people **without symptoms**; a man with symptoms needs the **diagnostic pathway**. In primary care this starts with a **chest X-ray**, followed by urgent referral if the film is abnormal or suspicion stays high. Recurrent chest infections and loss of appetite in a long-term ex-smoker are red flags.
w: Wrong - symptomatic patients enter the diagnostic pathway, not routine screening.
Wrong - persistent cough with red flags must not be watched for 3 months.
Wrong - sputum cytology is insensitive and is not the first-line test.
Correct - CXR is the first primary-care test, then refer if abnormal or suspicion is high.
Wrong - spirometry may help later but must not delay assessment for cancer.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old man with a 45 pack-year smoking history is awaiting a hospital appointment for a right hilar mass seen on chest X-ray. He returns to the Klinik Kesihatan with 1 week of headache worse on bending, swelling of the face and right arm, and breathlessness. He has distended non-pulsatile neck veins and dilated veins over the upper chest. BP is 138/84 mmHg and SpO2 94%.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Right-sided heart failure from cor pulmonale
Superior vena cava obstruction by tumour
Angioedema from an ACE inhibitor
Cardiac tamponade from a malignant effusion
Pancoast tumour with Horner syndrome
mcq.e: Facial and arm swelling, headache worse on bending and **distended non-pulsatile neck veins** with chest-wall collaterals are classic for **SVC obstruction**, most often from lung cancer (especially small-cell) or lymphoma compressing the vein. It is an oncological emergency needing same-day referral for imaging and treatment. Non-pulsatile veins and a normal BP help separate it from heart failure and tamponade.
w: Wrong - cor pulmonale causes ankle oedema and a pulsatile raised JVP, not facial and arm swelling.
Correct - tumour compressing the SVC gives facial and arm swelling with non-pulsatile neck veins.
Wrong - angioedema swells the lips and tongue and does not cause dilated chest veins.
Wrong - tamponade causes hypotension, pulsus paradoxus and a raised JVP that rises on inspiration.
Wrong - a Pancoast tumour gives shoulder pain, Horner syndrome and hand weakness.

mcq.stem:
A 59-year-old man who has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 38 years is eligible for lung cancer screening. Before referral for low-dose CT at a Klinik Kesihatan, he asks what he should expect.
Which statement is accurate counselling?
o: A normal scan means he can keep smoking safely
LDCT has no radiation, so yearly scans carry no risk
A chest X-ray each year would be just as effective
Any nodule found means he definitely has cancer
