Small nodules are common and most prove benign
mcq.e: LDCT reduces lung cancer deaths in high-risk smokers but has harms: **false positives** (indeterminate nodules are common and mostly benign), overdiagnosis, incidental findings and a low radiation dose. Screening never replaces **smoking cessation**, which remains the most effective intervention. Chest X-ray screening has not been shown to reduce mortality.
w: Wrong - screening is not a substitute for quitting; cessation must be offered at every visit.
Wrong - LDCT uses a low but real radiation dose.
Wrong - CXR screening has not reduced lung cancer deaths; LDCT is the recommended test.
Wrong - most screen-detected nodules are benign and are followed with surveillance scans.
Correct - false positives are common, so he should expect possible follow-up scans.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with mild nocturia. DRE reveals a hard, irregular nodule in the left lobe with loss of the median sulcus. His PSA, taken before the examination, is 2.8 ng/mL. Urinalysis is normal and there is no bone pain.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer urgently to urology for suspected prostate cancer
Reassure him, as the PSA is well within the normal range
Start tamsulosin and repeat the DRE in 6 months
Repeat the PSA in 3 months and refer if it rises
Start finasteride to shrink the nodule, then review it
mcq.e: A **hard, nodular prostate** or **loss of the median sulcus** on DRE needs urgent urology referral **regardless of PSA**, because some clinically significant cancers have a normal PSA. Repeating the PSA or treating as BPH delays diagnosis. 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors also halve the PSA, masking later results.
w: Correct - an abnormal DRE alone is an indication for urgent referral.
Wrong - a normal PSA does not exclude cancer when the DRE is abnormal.
Wrong - treating as BPH ignores a malignant-feeling prostate.
Wrong - waiting for the PSA to rise delays diagnosis of a palpable tumour.
Wrong - finasteride does not treat cancer and halves the PSA, masking it.

mcq.stem:
A 67-year-old man was treated at a Klinik Kesihatan 10 days ago for a febrile urinary tract infection, which has now resolved. A PSA taken on the day he presented was 11.4 ng/mL; he has no previous PSA. DRE today shows a smooth, mildly enlarged, non-tender prostate.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer urgently for prostate biopsy based on this PSA
Give a further 6 weeks of ciprofloxacin, then recheck
Repeat the PSA 6 weeks after the infection settles
Accept the result and add it to his BPH monitoring
Request a bone scan to exclude metastatic disease
mcq.e: Urinary infection and prostatitis raise PSA, often markedly, and the level can take several weeks to fall. Retest **at least 6 weeks after the infection has resolved** (and after 48 hours without ejaculation or vigorous exercise) before acting. If the repeat PSA is still above the age-specific threshold, refer to urology.
w: Wrong - a PSA taken during infection is unreliable and may lead to an unnecessary biopsy.
Wrong - the infection has resolved; extra antibiotics are not a way to treat a PSA value.
Correct - retesting after the infection settles avoids a false-positive result.
Wrong - an unexplained PSA of 11.4 ng/mL cannot simply be attributed to BPH.
Wrong - staging scans are not indicated before a reliable PSA or a diagnosis.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old man has taken dutasteride 0.5 mg daily for 2 years for a 60 mL benign-feeling prostate. Before treatment his PSA was 2.4 ng/mL. A routine PSA today is 2.6 ng/mL. DRE is unchanged and the prostate remains smooth.
How should this PSA be interpreted?
o: Reassuring, as it is unchanged from the baseline level
Concerning, as it equals about 5.2 ng/mL off treatment
Reassuring, as dutasteride has no effect on the PSA level
Concerning only if it rises above 10 ng/mL on treatment
Uninterpretable, so PSA should not be checked on dutasteride
mcq.e: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors roughly **halve PSA** after about 6 months, so the measured value should be **doubled** for interpretation. A PSA that stays flat or rises on dutasteride means the true value has roughly doubled, which raises concern for cancer and warrants urology review. Always take a baseline PSA before starting a 5-ARI.
w: Wrong - an unchanged PSA on a 5-ARI means the adjusted value has doubled.
Correct - doubling gives about 5.2 ng/mL, a real rise needing urology review.
Wrong - dutasteride lowers PSA by about 50%.
Wrong - waiting for 10 ng/mL ignores the halving effect and delays referral.
Wrong - PSA remains useful on a 5-ARI if the value is doubled.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man attending a Klinik Kesihatan health screen asks to 'add the prostate test' to his blood tests. He has no urinary symptoms, no family history of prostate cancer and a normal general examination.
What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Decline, as PSA testing is not allowed under the age of 60
Add the PSA without discussion, as he has asked for it
Advise a yearly PSA for life so that cancer is never missed
Discuss PSA benefits and harms, then decide together
Arrange a prostate MRI instead, as it is more accurate
mcq.e: PSA testing in a man without symptoms is an individual decision after **informed discussion**. He should hear that PSA can detect cancer early but gives false positives and negatives, can lead to biopsy and its complications, and may find slow-growing cancers that would never harm him (**overdiagnosis and overtreatment**). If he still wishes, test with a plan for acting on the result.
w: Wrong - there is no age bar at 60; informed testing is offered to men from about 50.
Wrong - testing without counselling skips consent about false positives and overdiagnosis.
Wrong - lifelong yearly testing increases overdiagnosis and is not recommended.
Correct - shared decision-making after explaining benefits and harms is standard.
Wrong - MRI is a specialist test after a raised PSA, not a screening tool.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer on hormone therapy attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 weeks of worsening thoracic back pain, worse lying flat, and since yesterday heavy legs and difficulty climbing stairs. Examination shows bilateral leg weakness (power 4/5) and brisk knee reflexes. He is passing urine normally.
What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Same-day referral for whole-spine MRI and oncology
Prescribe stronger analgesia and review in one week
Arrange outpatient physiotherapy for back strengthening
Request a routine bone scan and next oncology clinic
Repeat the PSA and refer if it has risen since last time
mcq.e: New back pain with leg weakness in a man with prostate cancer is **metastatic spinal cord compression** until proven otherwise. It needs **same-day** referral for whole-spine MRI and urgent treatment (high-dose dexamethasone, radiotherapy or surgery); waiting for bladder or bowel symptoms risks permanent paralysis. Function at the time of treatment predicts the outcome.
w: Correct - suspected cord compression needs emergency MRI and oncology review the same day.
Wrong - analgesia alone delays treatment while paralysis progresses.
Wrong - physiotherapy is inappropriate for possible cord compression.
Wrong - a routine bone scan does not image the cord and wastes time.
Wrong - the PSA does not change the need for emergency imaging.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old man is referred from a Klinik Kesihatan to urology with a PSA of 7.8 ng/mL, confirmed on repeat testing 6 weeks later. He has no urinary infection and DRE is smooth. The urologist explains the next step in the diagnostic pathway.
Which investigation is most likely to be done next?
o: Isotope bone scan for metastatic disease
CT of the abdomen and pelvis for staging
Free PSA and PSA velocity over a year
Cystoscopy to inspect the prostatic urethra
Multiparametric MRI of the prostate gland
mcq.e: Current EAU guidance, as on the slides, places **multiparametric MRI before biopsy** in men with a raised PSA. MRI identifies suspicious areas for targeted TRUS-guided or transperineal biopsy and can spare some men an unnecessary biopsy. Staging imaging (bone scan, CT) follows only after a histological diagnosis and risk grouping.
w: Wrong - a bone scan is for staging after diagnosis in higher-risk disease.
Wrong - CT staging comes after a biopsy-proven diagnosis.
Wrong - waiting a year for PSA velocity delays the diagnosis.
Wrong - cystoscopy is for haematuria and does not assess cancer within the gland.
Correct - mpMRI comes before biopsy to target suspicious lesions.

mcq.stem:
A 69-year-old man with hypertension has just been diagnosed with prostate cancer on targeted biopsy: ISUP Grade Group 1 (Gleason 3+3) in 2 of 12 cores, PSA 5.6 ng/mL and an impalpable tumour. MRI shows no spread beyond the prostate. He returns to his Klinik Kesihatan to ask about the options.
Which management is most appropriate for him to consider first?
o: Androgen deprivation therapy started straight away
Docetaxel chemotherapy to prevent further spread
Active surveillance with PSA, MRI and repeat biopsy
Palliative care referral for symptom control
Bilateral orchidectomy to remove testosterone
mcq.e: Low-risk localised prostate cancer (Grade Group 1, PSA under 10, organ-confined) often grows slowly, so **active surveillance** is preferred for suitable men, with radical treatment only if the disease progresses. This avoids the incontinence and erectile dysfunction of prostatectomy or radiotherapy. ADT and chemotherapy are for advanced or metastatic disease.
w: Wrong - ADT is for advanced disease and causes metabolic, bone and sexual side effects.
Wrong - chemotherapy is reserved for advanced, metastatic disease.
Correct - low-risk localised cancer is best managed with active surveillance.
Wrong - this is curable low-risk disease, not a palliative situation.
Wrong - surgical castration is a treatment for advanced disease only.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan for his first health screen. He has never smoked, drinks no alcohol and has no symptoms. BMI is 27 kg/m2 and BP 128/80 mmHg. He wants a 'cancer check' and asks which test is worth doing.
Which cancer screening test should be offered routinely?
o: A yearly chest X-ray to detect lung cancer
Serum CEA and AFP as a tumour marker panel
A PSA test without any prior discussion
Low-dose CT of the thorax as a baseline
Faecal immunochemical test (iFOBT)
mcq.e: Colorectal cancer is the commonest cancer in Malaysian men and screening reduces CRC deaths, so average-risk adults aged **50-75** are offered **iFOBT**, with colonoscopy if positive. Chest X-ray screening does not reduce deaths, LDCT is only for high-risk smokers, and tumour markers are not screening tests. PSA is offered only after informed discussion.
w: Wrong - CXR screening has not been shown to reduce lung cancer deaths.
Wrong - CEA and AFP are insensitive and are not screening tests.
Wrong - PSA testing requires shared decision-making first.
Wrong - LDCT is for long-term smokers aged 45-75, and he has never smoked.
Correct - iFOBT is the routine CRC screening test from age 50.

mcq.stem:
A Family Medicine Specialist reviews why men in her district rarely attend Klinik Kesihatan health screening. A survey shows most are daily-paid factory workers who say screening runs only during their working hours and the queue takes half a day.
Which intervention best addresses this barrier?
o: Run screening at the factories or in evening sessions
Put up more screening posters in the clinic waiting area
Send letters warning that unscreened men lose benefits
Offer screening only to men who already have symptoms
Ask their wives to book appointments in clinic hours
mcq.e: The barrier here is **system-related**: inconvenient hours and slow, complicated processes. The slides recommend **bringing screening closer to men**, male-friendly services and digital tools such as online booking. Posters inside the clinic reach only men who already attend.
w: Correct - workplace or out-of-hours screening removes the access barrier.
Wrong - posters in the clinic reach only those already attending.
Wrong - threats are unethical and do not fix the access problem.
Wrong - screening is aimed at people without symptoms.
Wrong - this does not change the clinic hours, which are the real barrier.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old taxi driver attends a Klinik Kesihatan asking only for 'a pill for erections'. He has had gradual-onset erectile difficulty for a year and has not seen a doctor for 10 years. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. BMI is 31 kg/m2, waist 104 cm and BP 146/94 mmHg.
Besides addressing his ED, what is the most important next step?
o: Prescribe sildenafil and ask him to return only if needed
Refer to urology for a penile Doppler ultrasound first
Screen now for diabetes, dyslipidaemia and hypertension
Check serum prolactin before considering any treatment
Arrange an exercise stress test before any treatment
mcq.e: Gradual-onset ED is often vascular and may precede coronary events by several years, so it is an **entry point for cardiovascular risk screening**. He needs HbA1c or fasting glucose, lipids, repeat BP readings and smoking cessation advice. Men rarely attend for check-ups, so this visit is an important opportunity.
w: Wrong - treating the symptom alone misses his likely vascular risk factors.
Wrong - Doppler is a specialist test that rarely changes primary-care management.
Correct - ED is a CVD marker, so screen for diabetes, lipids and hypertension.
Wrong - prolactin is checked when low libido or hypogonadism is suspected, not first.
Wrong - stress testing is for men with cardiac symptoms or high risk, not routine before treating ED.

mcq.stem:
A 47-year-old man is seen at a workplace health screen run by the Klinik Kesihatan. He feels well and says he does not think he is at risk of anything. A single seated BP after 5 minutes' rest is 152/96 mmHg. He has no symptoms, no diabetes and urinalysis is normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start amlodipine today, as one raised reading is diagnostic
Reassure him, as readings under 160/100 need no follow-up
Refer to a physician to exclude secondary hypertension
Confirm with repeat clinic or home BP readings first
Recheck the BP only at next year's workplace screen
mcq.e: A single raised reading at a screen does not establish hypertension. The diagnosis needs **repeated readings on separate occasions** or home/ambulatory BP monitoring, together with an assessment of overall cardiovascular risk. Many men have undiagnosed hypertension, so the result must not be ignored either.
w: Wrong - drug treatment follows confirmation unless BP is very high or there is organ damage.
Wrong - stage 1 readings still need confirmation and follow-up.
Wrong - secondary causes are considered in young, resistant or severe cases, not first.
Correct - repeat clinic or home readings confirm the diagnosis before treatment.
Wrong - a year's delay misses the chance to treat confirmed hypertension.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man brings his wife to a Klinik Kesihatan for her diabetes review. When offered a health screen himself, he declines, saying 'If they find something, I would rather not know.' He has no symptoms and has not had a check-up for many years.
What is the most appropriate response?
o: Accept the refusal and record that screening was declined
Explore his fears and explain early disease is treatable
Warn him firmly that men who avoid check-ups die younger
Ask his wife to persuade him to attend at a later date
Refer him to a psychiatrist to assess his health anxiety
mcq.e: **Fear of being diagnosed** is a common personal barrier to screening in men. A brief, non-judgemental discussion that explores his concerns and explains that screening finds treatable problems (raised BP, diabetes, early colorectal cancer) when outcomes are better respects his autonomy while addressing the barrier. Scare tactics, or involving others without his consent, tend to backfire.
w: Wrong - refusal can be respected, but only after his concerns have been explored.
Correct - addressing his fear of diagnosis is the key to engaging him.
Wrong - fear-based messages often increase avoidance.
Wrong - handing the decision to his wife bypasses his own autonomy.
Wrong - avoidance due to fear is not a psychiatric disorder needing referral.
